In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Naba' (Chapter of the Great News)

It is also called Surat 'Amma, and 'Amma yatasa'alun, and al-Tasa'ul, and al-Mu'sirat. It is Makki (Meccan) by consensus. Its verses number forty-one according to the Meccan and Basran counts, and forty according to others. The connection of this surah with what precedes it is that it affirms the power to resurrect, which the preceding surah indicated the unbelievers had denied. As for the link in the arrangement of the pearls (of the Qur'an), it lies in the similarity of its sentences to those of the preceding surah. In that surah there is: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾, ﴿Did We not create you from a degraded fluid?﴾, ﴿Did We not make the earth a receptacle?﴾, and so on. In this surah there is: ﴿Did We not make the earth a bed?﴾, and so on. In addition, it shares with the four preceding surahs the description of Paradise and Hell and what the one wrapped in garments (al-Muddaththir) was promised. Also, in Surat al-Mursalat there is: ﴿For what day has it been postponed?﴾, ﴿For the Day of Decision﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾, and in this surah: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time﴾, and so on. Thus this surah explains the Day of Decision, whose mention was mentioned in summary in what came before it. Ended quote from al-Alusi.

It has been said: when Allah, Exalted is He, concluded that (preceding) surah with His saying, ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾, and the "statement" there meant the Qur'an, He opened this surah by magnifying the questioning about it and mocking it. This is based on what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, that "the great news" means the Qur'an. The majority, however, hold that it is the Resurrection, and this is more suitable to the verses that follow, as you will know, Allah willing.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿'Amma﴾: its original form is 'an ma, with the preposition "'an" (about) entering upon the interrogative "ma" (what). The alif was dropped, and the reason given is to distinguish it from the relative (khabariyyah) "ma", and to signal the strength of the connection and the frequency of its use. The grammarians' reasons are well known. 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), Ubayy (Ibn Ka'b), 'Ikrimah and 'Isa (ibn 'Umar) read it with the alif, following the original form, though this is rarely used. Ibn Jinni said: retaining the alif is the weaker of the two dialects. Upon this is the line of verse:

"Why did he rise to revile me, that base one, like a pig that has rolled in ashes?"

The interrogation, by signaling the great importance of the subject asked about, and the fact that it is beyond the familiar categories, means: about what sort of thing of great importance?

﴿Yatasa'aluna﴾: the pronoun refers to the people of Makkah, even though they have not been mentioned before, because their presence is evident. Omitting their mention, as some have said, carries contempt and humiliation, since it implies that mentioning them is something the sanctuary of the Wise Reminder should be protected from. The reverse is not to be supposed, since the context prevents it. They used to ask one another about the Resurrection and discuss it, in denial and mockery. However, this was not a questioning about its reality and essence, but about its occurrence, which is one of its states and one of its attributes.

As has been mentioned more than once, "ma" is widely known for seeking the realities of things and the names of their referents, but it may also be used to seek the attribute or state, as in "What is Zayd?" and the answer is "A scholar" or "A physician." It has also been said: they used to question the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers, mockingly. In that case the verb "tasa'ala" is transitive, and its object is implied here, and it was omitted because it is evident, or because the one who magnifies the question does so regardless of who asked, or in order to protect the one asked about from being mentioned alongside this questioner. The realization of this, according to what is in al-Irshad (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, by Abu al-Su'ud), is that the form "tafa'ala" in transitive verbs indicates that the action proceeds from a plurality and falls upon them, such that each of them becomes both agent and object together. However, the plural is put in the nominative as the agent, giving preference to its agency, while its objecthood is left to be understood from the meaning of the verb, as in your saying: "tara'a al-qawm" (the people saw one another), meaning each of them saw the other. It may also be stripped of the second meaning, so that it signifies only the proceeding of the action from a plurality, without considering that it falls upon them. In that case, the verb takes an object, as in your saying: "tara'aw al-hilal" (they sighted the crescent). It may also be omitted, as in our case here. The meaning is: about what do these people ask the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers? Sometimes it may also be stripped of the proceeding of the action from a plurality, so that it signifies the plurality of its object while the agent is one, as in the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Then which of the favors of your Lord will you dispute?﴾.

Some scholars of verification have mentioned that the form "tafa'ala" in the first sense may also have an object, but a different one from the one who performed the act in the same manner, as in: "ta'ata al-ka's" (they passed the cup to one another), and "tafawada al-hadith" (they conversed mutually). Upon this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"When we disputed the talk, and she was gracious, I bent down a branch with clustered, swaying fruit."

Whoever says that "tafa'ala" is only from two parties and only intransitive has erred, as al-Batalyawsi said in his commentary on Adab al-Katib, if he intends this absolutely. How could that be right, when the use of "tafa'ala" in the sense of "fa'ala" with a single agent is very common, such as: "tawana Zayd" (Zayd delayed), "tada na al-amr" (the matter drew near), and "ta'ala Allahu 'amma yushrikun" (Allah is exalted above what they associate)? Likewise, its use transitively with an object other than the one who did the same act, as you have heard, is common.

It has also been allowed that the pronoun in ﴿yatasa'aluna﴾ refers to people in general, whether the unbelievers of Makkah or others among the Muslims. The questioning by the Muslims is for the sake of increasing their fear and faith, and the questioning by others is mockery, to increase their disbelief and rebellion. This, however, contradicts what the apparent meaning of the following verses requires.

It has been said: the questioning was about the Qur'an. This was objected to on the ground that the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Did We not make the earth...﴾ and so on, clearly shows that it was about the Resurrection. This is also narrated from Qatada, because it is one of its proofs. It was answered that their questioning about it, their mockery of it, and their disagreement over it, saying it was magic or poetry, was because it contained the announcement of the Resurrection. So after mentioning what conveys the magnitude of the questioning about it, the text addresses what is the source of that questioning, and in this there is some remoteness.

The discourse of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿About the Great News﴾ clarifies the status of the thing being asked about, after it has been magnified by leaving its matter undefined, directing the minds of the listeners towards it, and placing them in the position of those who ask. The mention of it in the form of a question by the Knower of the unseen is to alert that it is, because of its lacking any equal and having no like, beyond the circle of created knowledge, and is worthy of being cared about in knowing it and being asked about. It is as if it were said: "About what are they asking one another? Has He informed you of it?" Then it was said, by way of answer, ﴿About the Great News﴾, following the pattern of ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible.﴾

The phrase ﴿about﴾ (ʿan) is connected to what the mentioned [verb] indicates, namely a hidden element whose proper place, as it has been said, is to be estimated after it, for haste towards the clarification and for observing the order of the question. The one who went to connecting it with what has been mentioned is al-Zajjaj, and this is what the sublime quality of the revelation requires.

Makki said that this is a substitute (badal) for the interrogative *mā* (what), by repeating the preposition. Al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari's work) criticised this, saying that it is not sound, since the meaning of the first would be "about the great news, or about something other than it," and a substitute does not match it; the interrogation was repeated at first.

Al-Khafaji said: the substitution is permissible, and the interrogation need not be repeated, because it is not a true interrogation; nor must the substitute be identical to the first, since it may be a substitute of part [of the whole].

It has also been said that it is connected to the mentioned ﴿they ask one another﴾, and ﴿about what﴾ is connected to a hidden element that is explained by it. This is reinforced by the reading of al-Dahhak, Yaʿqub and Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, as ʿammah with the hā' al-sakt (the pausal hā'), and its explanation is that it is in pause, and this indicates that it is not connected to what was mentioned, because a pause is not good between the preposition and its object and what is connected to it, since the sentence is not complete. Perhaps the one who went to the first view would say: the addition of the hā' is based on treating the continuous reading as if it were a pause.

It has also been said: the first *ʿan* is for causation (taʿlil, stating the reason), and it and the second are both connected to the mentioned ﴿they ask one another﴾, as if it were said: "Why do they ask one another about the Great News?" Ibn ʿAtiyya related this from the majority of the grammarians.

It has also been said: ﴿about the news﴾ is connected to an omitted element, and there is a hidden interrogation, as if it were said: ﴿About what do they ask one another?﴾ Is it [that] they ask one another ﴿about the Great News﴾? The news, which is the report that has a great matter, was described as ﴿great﴾ to emphasise its importance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 3:

He described it by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿About which they differ﴾, for emphasis in that matter and to signal that the questioning revolves around it. The word "fihi" (about it) is connected to ﴿differ﴾ and is placed before it out of concern for it and for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil). Making the relative clause a nominal sentence indicates permanence; that is, they are firmly rooted in disagreement about it. Thus, one who is certain of its impossibility says: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world; we die and we live﴾, etc. And one who doubts says: ﴿We do not know what the Hour is. We only assume an assumption, and we are not certain﴾. It has also been said: among them are those who deny both the resurrection and the return, like these; and among them are those who deny only the bodily resurrection, like the majority of the Christians. The disagreement has been interpreted as a disagreement in the manner of denial: among them are those who deny it because they deny the Maker, who chooses, exalted is His majesty, and among them are those who deny it on the basis of the impossibility of restoring what has ceased to exist in its very same identity. It has also been said: the disagreement is between affirmation and denial, or in the increase of fear and mockery, on the basis that the pronoun in ( they question one another ) and their pronoun refer to people in general. It has also been said: the disagreement may be between affirmation and denial, with the pronoun in ( they question one another ) referring also to the disbelievers, by taking their pronoun as referring to the questioners and the questioned, all together. And all of this, as you see, though the degrees of weakness differ, and the first is the one relied upon.

The Mufti of the Ottoman lands said: What verification requires and careful reflection demands is that their disagreement about the resurrection be understood as their opposition to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him; by considering in the disagreement the mere occurrence of the act from more than one party, as has been said regarding the questioning. For the form of ifti'al and the form of tafa'ul are sister forms, like istibaq and tasabuq, and intidal and tanadul, and what applies to one of them applies to the other. This is not on the basis of some of them opposing others, such that each side is both an opposer (ism fa'il) and one opposed (ism maf'ul). For although all deserve what is mentioned afterward of rebuke and threat, the deserving of each side of these is not because it opposes the other side, since there is no rightness in either of them such that whoever opposes it deserves blame. Rather, it is because it opposes him, upon him be prayer and peace. So it is as if it were said: "About which they are opposers" to the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. End of quote. But this is contrary to the apparent meaning, and what he mentioned as reasoning is not free from some difficulty. Abdullah and Ibn Jubayr read "tassa'aluna" without the ya' and with a shaddah on the sin, on the basis that its original form is "tatasa'aluna" with the taa' of address, and the second taa' was assimilated into the sin.

﴿Nay﴾ is a deterrent from the questioning in the two aspects previously mentioned. It was also said that it refers to that questioning and to the disagreement, meaning opposition to the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the matter of resurrection. This was criticized on the grounds that the sentence containing it was not intended for its own sake, so it is far-fetched to take the deterrence as applying to what is in it. His words, glorified is He, ﴿They will come to know﴾, are a warning to those questioners who mock, by way of isti'naf (a new sentence not grammatically dependent on what precedes), and an explanation of the deterrence. The sīn is for proximity and emphasis. The object of "they will know" is omitted; it is what they will encounter of kinds of calamities and punishments. The expression of meeting it with knowledge is because it occurs in the context of questioning. The meaning is: so that they desist from what they are upon, for they will come to know soon the reality of the situation when punishment and torment befall them. Similar to this is assuming the object as the recompense of the questioning. It was also said that the object is what the apparent context indicates, namely the occurrence of what they question about, meaning: they will know that, and they will be embarrassed by their questioning and mockery before their Lord, Mighty and Majestic; otherwise it would not appear that what was mentioned is a warning. As for the one who made the pronoun in ﴿they question﴾ refer to people generally, he treated what is here as an instance of taghlib (predominance of one group over another within a general term), because it is directed at those who do not firmly believe in resurrection. Some allowed that ﴿Nay, they will come to know﴾ be both a deterrent and a promise, on the condition of desisting; the meaning being: so that they desist, for they will come to know the rewards of desisting. You know that this is common in warnings, and it is what is understood from it in such contexts.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 5:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then, nay, they will come to know﴾. It was said: it is a repetition of what preceded it, of the deterrence and warning, for the sake of emphasis. And ﴿thumma﴾ (then) indicates a difference in rank, as if it were said: for them on the Day of Resurrection there is a deterrence and a severe punishment, nay, for them on that day there is what is more and more severe. On this basis, it becomes as if it were different from what precedes it, so it is coordinated with it. Ibn Malik says of such a case that it is verbal emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi), even if a conjunction intervenes, so do not be heedless.

It was also said: the first refers to what occurs at the extraction and departure of the soul, from the rebuke of the angels of death, peace be upon them, and the encounter with the agonies and severities of death, and the lifting of the veil. The second refers to what occurs on the Resurrection, from the rebuke of the angels of punishment, peace be upon them, and the encounter with severe retribution. So ﴿thumma﴾ is in its proper place, because of the temporal distance between them, and there is no repetition in it.

The apparent view is that the coordination, according to this and what precedes it, is with the whole of ﴿nay, they will come to know﴾. Some people, from the speech of some of the eminent scholars, supposed that the coordination is with (sa-ya'lamun, "they will come to know"). It was objected that if ﴿thumma﴾ is for temporal succession, it requires separating the coordinated item from the item it coordinates by something foreign, unlike when it is for rank-based succession. It was justified, to avoid specification without a specifier, that on the second view it is understood that there is a difference in rank between the two deterrences, just as there is between the two warnings, since the deterrence follows the warning. Thus the second ﴿kalla﴾ (nay) is not foreign. By contrast, on the first view, succession occurs only where time occurs, and there is nothing but (sa-ya'lamun) without (kalla), so the latter would be foreign. Then that same person who supposed this said: it is not far-fetched to say that the first deterrence is against questioning, and the second is against outright denial. The difference between them requires coordination with ﴿thumma﴾. All of this, as you see, [is weak].

It was also said: the object of knowing in the first is the resurrection, and in the second it is the requital for denying it. And ﴿thumma﴾ is in its proper place, meaning: ﴿nay, they will come to know﴾ the reality of the resurrection when they are raised; ﴿then, nay, they will come to know﴾ the requital for denying it when they enter the Fire and are punished. It was permitted that the object be different, with ﴿thumma﴾ indicating rank-based succession, meaning: the disbelievers will come to know their own conditions, then they will come to know the conditions of the believers. The first refers to physical punishment, and the second to spiritual punishment, which is more severe and more humiliating. It was also permitted that the agent of (sa-ya'lamu, "he will come to know") be different in the two places, on the basis that the pronoun of (yatasa'aluna, "they question one another") refers to people in general, and ﴿thumma﴾ is likewise for this reason. The meaning would then be: the believers will come to know the outcome of their affirmation, then the disbelievers will come to know the outcome of their denial. The first is a promise to the believers and the second a threat to the disbelievers, and they differ in rank. What is in this is not hidden from you.

Malik ibn Dinar, Ibn Muqsim, al-Hasan and Ibn Amir read (sata'lamun, "you will come to know") in both places with the second-person ta' (taa' fawqiyya), in the manner of iltifat (shift) to address, in accordance with the address that follows it in the other addresses, to intensify the deterrence and warning. It is not on the assumption: "Say to them, nay, you will come to know," etc. For that is not the case, although there is some beauty in it on the assumption that what is meant is that they question the Prophet (ﷺ).

And from al-Dahhak, that he read the first with the ta' of address and the second with the ya' of the third person.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 6:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have We not made the earth a bed?﴾ and so on, it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought in to confirm the tidings about which they were questioning, by enumerating some of the evidences that speak to its truth, after alerting to them through what was mentioned of the rebuke (radc). It is also permissible that it be with the implied verb "Say" (qul), as if it were said: "Say: How do you deny or doubt the Resurrection, when you have witnessed what points to it of complete power, all-encompassing knowledge, and dazzling wisdom, which requires that what has been created not be in vain?" In this there is that whoever is of great station and dazzling power should be feared, revered, and affected by his warning and threat. The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for affirmation (taqrir) of what follows a negation, and al-mihad means: the spread-out bedding (al-firash al-muwatta').

In al-Qamus: al-mahd is the place prepared for the infant, like al-mihad. Accordingly, al-mahd and al-mihad have the same meaning. This is supported by the reading of Mujahid and Isa al-Hamdani, "mahdan." In the verse, in that case, there is an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh). Each of the two is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a name for what is spread out. It is also permissible that it remain as a verbal noun, and describing with a verbal noun is common; or that it be taken as an implied "possessor of a bed or cradle" (dhat mihad aw mahd). It has also been said: just as al-mihad can be a verbal noun used for the object, it may be the form fi'al, meaning a noun on its pattern taken for the object, like al-ilah (the deity) and al-imam (the leader). His making the earth a bed is either in its original creation or after it. Whichever it is, there is no indication in the verse of anything that contradicts its sphericity, as is well known from the several doctrines of the modern astronomers (ahl al-hay'a al-muhdathin) that it is flattened at the two poles, because it was extremely soft in the beginning owing to the extreme heat latent within it, which today is present in it at that time, and it has rotated on its axis; the combination of all this has required its becoming flattened at the two poles according to them. The people of the Sharia do not say this, and no proof for the one who says it is complete until God, Exalted is He, inherits the earth and whoever is upon it.

﴿And the mountains as pegs﴾. That is, like pegs. There is in this also an eloquent simile, and the meaning is: We fixed the earth firm with the mountains as a tent is fixed firm with pegs. Al-Afwah said:

"The house is not built except that it has pillars,
and there is no pillar if its pegs are not driven in."

It is related in a hadith: "God, exalted is He, created the earth and it began to sway, so He placed the mountains upon it and it became stable. The angels said: 'Our Lord, hast Thou created any creation harder than the mountains?' He said: 'Yes, iron.' They said: 'Our Lord, hast Thou created any creation harder than iron?' He said: 'Yes, fire.' They said: 'Our Lord, hast Thou created any creation harder than fire?' He said: 'Yes, water.' They said: 'Our Lord, hast Thou created any creation harder than water?' He said: 'Yes, wind.' They said: 'Our Lord, hast Thou created any creation harder than wind?' He said: 'Yes, the son of Adam, who gives charity with his right hand and conceals it from his left.'"

The apparent meaning, like that of others, is that the creation of the mountains came along with the creation of the earth, and this is the view of the earlier and later philosophers, though they differ among themselves as to their coming into being, earlier or later. In a hadith narrated by al-Hakim, who graded it sound, from Ibn Abbas: "The first mountain was Abu Qubays." As to the manner of their coming into being, since they came into existence, there is disagreement among them, and what has come into being of them may vanish with the passage of time:

"When the two new things (night and day) succeed one another
over a new thing, they deliver it to decay."

It is sometimes observed that some rocky hills come into being from the freezing of some waters. It has been raised as an objection that their need to be fixed by mountains conflicts with their tendency toward the center because of their absolute weight. It is answered that God, exalted is He, knew that they would be, and that there would be upon them what weights there would be. It is known that in that case they would have two centers: a center of volume and a center of weight. The one that coincides with the center of the world is only the center of weight. Thus, if a heavy thing moves toward the east or the west, for example, upon them, their movement follows from the shift of their center of weight and the necessity of its coinciding with the center of the world, so swaying occurs. At that time they were not in such a state that, given the weights upon them, their stillness would have a perceptible measure, so the mountains were placed upon them, the center of their weight coincided with the center of the world, and the whole of the earth and the mountains became such that after a certain amount, it does not appear to what moves it in a way that is perceptible. It has also been said: they were so light that the waves of the surrounding ocean would move them and swaying would occur, so they were made heavy by the mountains, along with the many benefits in the mountains for which the earth was not created, such that the waves do not move it. The full discussion of this, as far as we have been informed, has already passed, so recall it. It is related of some that making it so means making it a cause for the orderly arrangement of the people of the earth through what was deposited in it of benefits, and that without them it would have swayed with them. That is, it would not have been ready for benefiting from it, and the affair of their dwelling upon it would have been disturbed. This is an interpretation contrary to the apparent meanings, and it is not needed as long as no conclusive proof has established the impossibility of the apparent meaning being intended. Indeed, it has been said that this is closer to the established sense, for making them pegs in this meaning is more evident than making them so in that meaning, and closer to knowing it. It may also be said that it fits better with not repeating the governing verb. Whoever does not see it so takes the point in it to be the strength of the connection and association between the earth and the mountains. Understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 8:

﴿And We created you⁠﴾ is conjoined to the negated present-tense verb with "lam" (lam), and it falls under its ruling; for it carries the sense of "either We made..." (etc.). Or it is conjoined to what the rebuking denial (al-inkar al-taqriri) requires, for it carries the sense of saying: "Indeed We have made..." (etc.). The turn to address (al-iltifat ila al-khitab) here is based on the well-known reading in ﴿they will know﴾ (sa-ya'lamun),

for the sake of emphasis in the binding argument and rebuke. ﴿In pairs﴾ (azwajan). Al-Zajjaj and others said: paired, male and female, so that procreation may be possible and the affairs of livelihood may be ordered. It was also said: kinds differing in color, form and language. It was also said: it is permissible that the intended meaning of the creation in pairs is the creation from two fluids, the fluid of the man and the fluid of the woman, so that We created each one of you in pairs by reference to its matter, which is an expression for two fluids. Thus ﴿We created you in pairs﴾ would be of the type of setting plural against plural and distributing individuals over individuals, and this is extremely contrary to the apparent meaning, and there is no reason for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 9:

﴿And We made your sleep a subat (a state of rest and cessation).﴾ That is, like subat. In the speech there is an eloquent simile, as has already been mentioned. The meaning of subat here is death, and this sense is attested in the lexicon. The basis for likening sleep to it is evident. On this same basis is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who takes you back to Himself by night.﴾ The word subat, on the pattern of ad'a' (ailments), is derived from sabt (cutting off), because it involves the cessation of work and movement. It is said: sabata sha'rahu (he shaved his hair) when he shaved it, and anfahu (he cut off his nose) when he cut it off entirely. Ibn al-Anbari, as cited in al-Durar, claimed that he had not heard sabt in the sense of cutting off, and it seems he was deaf. It has also been said: the original meaning of sabt is stretching out, like spreading, as one says: sabata al-sha'r (he loosened the hair from its braids). On this basis, subat is interpreted as long, extended sleep, and the favour of it lies in the absence of disturbance. Some have permitted interpreting it as light sleep, based on what is in al-Qamus regarding its application to that, so that the meaning would be: We made your sleep light, not extended, whereby the affairs of your livelihood and your return would be disrupted. In al-Bahr, subat means tranquillity and rest; it is said: sabata al-rajul (the man rested) when he rested. Ibn al-Anbari also claimed that sabata in this sense is not attested, and al-Murtada refuted him, saying that what is meant is the rest that necessarily accompanies sleep and the cessation of sensation; for in that is the rest of the animal faculties from the fatigue that befalls them while awake. From this, the well-known day was named Saturday (sabt), because of the leisure and rest they have in it. It has also been said that it was named thus because God, Exalted is He, began the creation of the heavens and the earth on Sunday, and created them in six days as He mentioned, and then He, glorified is He, ceased His work on Saturday, so it was named accordingly. The verifying scholars chose that subat here means death, because it is more fitting to the context, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 10:

﴿And We made the night﴾ (the time in which sleep commonly occurs) ﴿a garment﴾, which covers you with its darkness as clothing covers you. Perhaps the intended "garment" to which the night is compared is that with which one covers oneself during sleep, such as a blanket and the like; for the resemblance of the night to it is more complete, and its consideration in achieving the purpose is more fitting. Yet more than one scholar has preferred the broader meaning, that the sense is: We made it a cover for you from eyes when you wish to flee from an enemy, or to attack him by night, or to conceal what you do not want to be seen, of the many matters [of that kind].

Al-Mutanabbi counted among the blessings of the night the attack upon enemies by night, and the attainment of visiting the beloved and meeting, refuting what is well known of the doctrine of the Manichaeans, that goodness is ascribed to light and evil to darkness in the known sense. He said:

"How many a favour darkness of the night has done me, which proves that the Manichaeans lie."

"Night saved you from the enemies' ruin as you journeyed toward them, and the veiled one of coquetry visited you in it."

Some have said: it is possible to interpret the night's being like a garment as its being like a garment for the day in the ease of bringing it out, and from it [the phrase "And We made the night..."]. Its remoteness is not hidden. Among what is truly astonishing is the argument of some who cite this verse as proof that whoever prays naked at night or in darkness, his prayer is valid. By my life, he has indeed come up with a nakedness devoid of the garment of verification, as is not hidden to one upon whom the light of the Truth, the Real, has dawned.

﴿وجَعَلْنا النَّهارَ مَعاشًا﴾ *Ma'āsh* is a *maṣdar mīmī* (a verbal noun formed with an initial *mīm*, a form that denotes the place or state of the action) meaning *al-ʿaysh* (living), which is life specific to animals, according to what al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said, as distinct from the general sense of life, as in the life of a king, for example. It functions here as an adverbial of time (*ẓarf*), as it is said in examples like: *ataytuka khufūqa al-najm wa ṭulūʿa al-fajr* ("I came to you at the twinkling of the star and the rising of dawn"). It was also permitted that it be a noun of time (*ism zamān*), but this was objected to on the grounds that its occurrence in this way has not been established in the language. The meaning is: "And We made the day a time of living," that is, a life in which you are roused from your sleep, which is the brother of death. It seems that when He, glorified is He, made sleep a metaphorical death, He, majestic is His glory, made wakefulness a livelihood in the same way; but the day was chosen to match the intermediate (*al-mutawassiṭ*). It was also said that the meaning is: "And We made the day a time of livelihood in which you move about to obtain what you live by." This is more fitting with making *al-subāt* (rest/cessation) in what preceded mean cessation from movement, as it is said. The excellence of mentioning the making of the night a garment after the making of sleep a *subāt* is not hidden, and it points to the wisdom of making sleep at night too, since the sleeper's senses are inactive, so he is in need of a covering against what would harm him; hence he is most in need of a wrapping and of pitching the tents of concealment. In *al-Kashshāf* it is stated that the antithesis (*muṭābaqa*) between His saying, exalted is He, ﴿وجَعَلْنا اللَّيْلَ لِباسًا﴾ and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿وجَعَلْنا النَّهارَ مَعاشًا﴾ is explicit, and there is also a semantic antithesis in it with His saying, exalted is He, (And We made sleep...), in that the day is the time of wakefulness and livelihood, in opposition to *al-subāt*, because it is the movement of the living. From this it is known that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿وجَعَلْنا اللَّيْلَ لِباسًا﴾ is not a digression (*mustaṭrad*). The arrangement (*wajh al-naẓm*) is that when He mentioned their creation in pairs (*azwājan*), He completed their states, both when together and when apart. End. In this there is an indirect criticism (*taʿrīḍ*) of al-Ṭībī, since he claimed a digression when the livelihood is meant as wakefulness and the *subāt* as death.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 12:

﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens]﴾. That is: seven heavens, strong in their creation, firmly made, none of which falls down upon you, which would prevent you from making a living. The expression of their creation by "building" is to indicate their resemblance to domes built over a resting place. It has also been said: it is to indicate that their creation was gradual, but this is not the case. In it [this verse] is [an indication] that the heaven is tent-like (khaymiyyah), not a level flat surface, and in the reports there is what bears witness to this and does not contradict it, [namely the verse] "We made it a ceiling" in another verse. And it is authentically reported in the Hadith of the 'Arsh (Throne) what also bears witness to it being tent-like. The earlier philosophers [hold] that it is spherical, and they call it the falak (celestial sphere). They argued for this according to their principles, after arguing for the sphericity of the apparent surface of the earth, and no proof for it is fully complete for them. They said: what indicates the sphericity of the heaven is that when we go to a number of dwellings along one line of latitude of the earth, and we obtain the stars passing directly over the head in each of them, then we consider the distances of the paths of those stars in the meridian circle from one another, we find them in the same ratios as the earthly distances between those dwellings. Likewise we find the elevation of the pole there varying by the same ratios. Thus the curvature of the heaven in the Throne is similar to the curvature of the earth in it. But this similarity exists along every line of latitude, and likewise along every line of longitude, so the entire surface of the heaven is parallel to the entire apparent surface of the earth, and this surface is sensibly spherical, so the surface of the heaven parallel to it is likewise [spherical]. Also, the astronomers recorded the magnitudes of the bodies of the stars and the distances between them in different places at one time, as at the midday of those places, [finding them] equal in certain cases, and this indicates the equality of the distances of the centres of the stars from the points of sight, which entails the equality of their distances from the centre of the world, owing to the sphericity of the earth, which entails that the heaven is spherical. They claimed that these two are the closest things to rely upon for sphericity from the standpoint of instructional reasoning, and in each there is a debate. As for the second, the objection to it is that it is only valid if the sphere was stationary according to them and the stars moving; for if the heaven were moving, it could be that it is square-shaped, and the equality of the distances of the centres of the stars from the points of sight and the equality of the magnitudes of the stars would still hold. As for the first, the objection to it is that it is only valid if the said equilibrium existed along every line of longitude and latitude, and this is not known. As for their other proofs apart from what has been mentioned, they are recorded, along with what is in them, in Nihayat al-Idrak fi Dirayat al-Aflak; return to it if you wish.

There remains here an issue: if the conjunction is upon the verb negated by lam, what falls under its ruling entails that the building of the seven strong heavens above you was known to the addressees, who are the polytheists of Makkah who deny the Resurrection, as you have heard, so that they can be made to acknowledge it as with the other matters before and after it. It is said: that the heavens are seven is among what cannot be perceived by observation, and they are those who denied the Prophet (ﷺ), so they would not believe him in such a thing whose knowledge, outwardly, comes only by way of revelation. It is answered: they knew it through observing the differences in the movements of the seven planets together with the differences in their distances from one another. For they knew the planets and the differences in their movements, and they knew that if some of them were above others, some would eclipse others; so they said at first glance: seven heavens, each heaven for one of these stars. We need not discuss what they said about the fixed stars and the mover of them and of the seven by the daily motion, for that lies beyond what we are concerned with. It has been objected that this is only valid if they were holding that the heaven is the celestial sphere, that it moves in a circular path, and that its apogee is its perigee and its perigee its apogee; but perhaps they do not say this, and they say, like some of the early Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), that the heaven is stationary and the star moves, and the falak is only its course. In that case it is possible that the seven, with their differing movements and distances, are within the thickness of one heaven, moving in orbits and courses of their own in the manner perceived by the senses; and other possibilities are also allowed, as is not hidden. Furthermore, if their knowledge of this were from what was mentioned, they would have spoken of epicycles and the like, as the earlier astronomers said, since differences in movement require them according to their claim, especially in the case of the wandering planet. And if the Arabs had held this, it would have occurred in their poetry; indeed, it is not far-fetched that if someone had mentioned to them epicycles and the enclosing and enclosed deferents, for example, they would have attributed it to what they dislike. It has also been said that they inherited knowledge of this from their forefathers who heard it from people whom they believed to be truthful, such as Isma'il (peace be upon him); and it is possible that they heard it from the People of the Book, and since they did not see it as contradicting what they held, they believed it; and this degree of knowledge suffices for the soundness of the statement. It was criticised: on this view the conjunctions by which they are grouped together under one heading of knowledge would not be coherent; but the matter is easy. It has also been said: they were treated as those who know it, because the evidence for it is manifest, namely the report of one whose truthfulness is established by a miracle concerning it; but this is far-fetched. It has also been said: the address is to people, believers and polytheists alike, and the believers were given precedence over the others in the affirmation, which implies prior knowledge; and this, as you see, is weak. Some have chosen that the conjunction is upon what the affirmative denial (al-inkar al-taqriri) implies, so that the statement carries the force of: "We have indeed made the earth..." to the end.

﴿And We built above you seven strong [heavens]﴾. In that case it is the beginning of an informative statement from Him, Mighty and Majestic, about the said building, and so it does not entail prior knowledge. It was criticised: that the conjunction upon the verb negated by "lam" is more suitable for reasoning from the things mentioned to the soundness of the Resurrection, as is not hidden; so reflect. The placing of the adverbial phrase before the object is for emphasis, and also in observance of the rhyming pauses (fawasil).

﴿And We made﴾, that is, We brought into being and originated, ﴿a blazing lamp﴾, shining and radiant. The word derives from *wahajat al-nar* (the fire blazed) when it gives light, or it means intensely hot, from *al-wahaj* (intense heat). What is meant is the sun. The expression of it as a lamp is one of the allusive expressions (*rawadif*) used for the creation of the heavens described as building.

*Sirajan* is in the accusative as the object, and *wahhajan* is in the accusative as its attribute. Some scholars permitted that both be objects of *al-ja'l* (making), since here the verb takes two objects. This was criticized as contrary to the apparent sense because both are indefinite. And even if it is said that *al-siraj* is the sun, and because it is restricted to a single instance it is like a definite noun, the objection still stands. There is disagreement about the place where the making occurred. The well-known view is that it is in the fourth heaven. We have found no report on this except what is in *al-Bahr* from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: "The sun is in the fourth heaven, its back facing us, and its flame blazes upward."

What is mentioned in the books of these people is that they posited seven spheres for the seven planets, arranged so that some eclipse others. The farthest is for Zuhal (Saturn), then the one beneath it for Mushtari (Jupiter), then for Mirrikh (Mars). The nearest is for the Moon, and above it is for Utarid (Mercury), then for Zuhra (Venus). They reached this because they found the Moon eclipsing six of the planets and many of the fixed stars situated along its path through the zodiac. On this arrangement, they found that the lower eclipses the higher, and the fixed stars are eclipsed by all of them. The eclipsing body is known from the eclipsed by the difference in color: whichever body's color appears during the eclipse is the eclipsing one, and whichever's color is hidden is the eclipsed one. Doubt remained about the sun, since no eclipse of the sun by any of the stars was known, because its light is overwhelmed by its brilliance when they come near it, and because it has never been eclipsed by any star other than the Moon.

Some of the early scholars therefore held that the spheres of Venus and Mercury are above the sphere of the sun, arguing that they do not eclipse it as the Moon does. This is false, because a condition for the lower eclipsing the higher is that the two be together and the sight lie on one straight line. Otherwise the lower does not eclipse the higher, as in most conjunctions of the Moon. If that is so, it is possible that their orbits lie between the sun and the eyes. Also, their bodies, according to them, are small and not dark like the body of the Moon, so that they would eclipse the sun. And if the Moon eclipses a portion of the sun's body equal in size to one of these two stars, or larger, the eclipsed part does not appear to the eyes, as Batlamyus (Ptolemy) explicitly stated in *al-Iqtisas*.

Some of those whose era is long past held that the two are beneath the sphere of the sun, even though they do not eclipse it, because of the fine order and excellent arrangement this implies, as explained in its proper place. Batlamyus also inclined to this view. In *al-Majisti* (the Almagest) he said: "We see the arrangement of those of long ago as closer to persuasion, because it resembles the natural order, the sun lying between what is farthest from it and what is only slightly distant from it. Then his resolve strengthened when he saw that the known distance of the sun from the earth was suitable for this position, because between the farthest distance of the Moon and the nearest proximity of the sun there is a distance in which the two spheres of Venus and Mercury and their differing distances can be placed."

In *al-Iqtisas* he said: "Such a space should not be left empty, and it is not fitting that Mars, let alone others, should be there. Therefore let those two be there." This was reinforced by some later scholars, who said that Venus was observed on the disc of the sun at two times about twenty-odd years apart. In the first of the two instances it was at the peak of its epicycle, and in the second at its lowest point. This refutes what was supposed about Mercury and Venus being in one sphere with the sun, and about the center of their epicycles, because Venus could not be seen at the peak in this way. These are weak arguments, some of them rhetorical and persuasive, and some of them have their flaws explained in their proper place.

Some people have claimed that just as there is an eclipse-mark on the face of the Moon, so on the face of the sun, a little above its center, there is a black spot. The astronomers today, as we have heard from more than one source, are certain that there is blackness and various markings on its disc, and they have statements about this recorded in their books. If that is so, then comparing the two to a lamp has much beauty. It is also reported from some of them that the light is like a tent over it, and I have seen in some of their books that it splits open around the edges of its body. As for the discussion of the size of its body and its distance from the earth, this is in the view of all the earlier and contemporary philosophers. We have no need of it in this place, especially with the disagreement that would lead, in explaining what is for and against it, to further lengthy discussion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 14:

﴿And We sent down from the squeezing clouds⦆ — they are the clouds, according to what has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Rabiʿ and al-Dahhak. Since the word muʿsirah (the form ending in -ah) is a passive participle (ism mafʿul) and not an active participle (ism fail), it has been said that it is the plural of muʿsirah from aʿsara, with the hamzah in it being for ḥaynunah (the sense of approaching a time), meaning: it has approached and is about to be squeezed by the winds so that it rains. The form if'āl (af'ala) often carries this meaning, as in judira (the animal was slaughtered) when the time of its slaughtering came, and uḥṣida (the crop was reaped) when it drew near the time of its harvest. From this comes aʿsarat al-jāriyah (the girl approached puberty) when she came near to menstruating. Abu al-Najm al-ʿIjli said:

She walks slowly, her headscarf slipping, for she has approached puberty, or her whirlwind of youth has drawn near.

It is also permitted, on the assumption that the hamzah is for ḥaynunah, that the meaning is: it is time for it to squeeze, i.e. to bring relief (tughīth); and from this comes al-ʿāsir, the one who brings relief. Therefore Ibn Kaysan said: the clouds were named so because they bring relief; they are from al-ʿaṣrah, as if originally in the sense of "it is time to squeeze," by imagining that blood is produced from them by squeezing. It has also been said that it is likewise a plural for this, except that the hamzah is for the becoming of the agent as possessing the quality, like aysar and aʿsar and alḥam, meaning: he became possessed of ease, became possessed of hardship, became possessed of flesh. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah that it is the winds, because they squeeze the clouds so that it rains. Some have explained it as the winds possessing whirlwinds (dhawāt al-aʿāsīr), with the form of the active participle being for the relative sense (nisbah) to al-iʿṣār (with a kasrah), which is a wind that stirs up a cloud containing thunder and lightning; and the abstraction (tajrīd) is considered in it, as has been said. Al-Mazini also considered the relative sense, but he said: "al-muʿṣirāt" are the clouds possessing whirlwinds, for they must rain along with them. He supported explaining it as the winds by the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn ʿAbbas, his brother al-Fadl, ʿAbdullah ibn Yazid, ʿIkrimah and Qatadah: "bi-l-muʿṣirāt" with the bāʾ of cause and instrumentality, for it is evident in the winds, since by them the water descends from the cloud. On the basis of this reading, some made the "min" in the reading of the majority, and the explanation of "al-muʿṣirāt" as the winds, to be for causation. Others held that it is for initial causation (ibtidāʾiyyah), since the cloud is like the originating agent of the descent; but it has been objected that the use of "min" in this way is rare. Also from Abu al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam, Muqatil and Qatadah, it is said that it means the heavens. It has been objected that water does not descend from the heaven by squeezing, so it was said in its interpretation: water descends from the heaven to the cloud, so it is as if the heavens are squeezed, i.e. are carried by the squeezing of the winds upon the cloud and are enabled to do so. It has been objected that, even with its remoteness, this only holds if al-muʿṣir came in the sense of al-ʿāsir, i.e. the one who causes squeezing; and if it were said that the intended meaning of al-muʿṣir is the one for whom the time has come to be squeezed, that would be a strained interpretation upon a strained interpretation. What is in al-Kashshaf is that the hamzah, on the aforementioned interpretation, is for transitivity; so reflect, and do not be heedless.

﴿Water pouring forth abundantly⦆ — i.e. poured out in abundance. It is said: thajja al-māʾ when water flowed abundantly, and thajjahu, i.e. he caused it to flow. Thajja occurs both intransitive and transitive, and it has been preferred to take what is in the noble text as intransitive, because that is the more common usage. al-Zajjaj took it as transitive, as if the water sent down, because of its abundance, pours itself out. From the transitive usage is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of Hajj is ʿajj and thajj." That is: raising the voice with the talbiyah and pouring out the blood of the sacrifice; and what is intended is that the best of the acts of Hajj are the talbiyah and the sacrifice. Abundance does not preclude the water being from the squeezing clouds, and its apparent meaning is that it is by squeezing, which yields only a little; but that is not accepted, and even if accepted, the scarcity is relative. Al-Aʿraj read: "thajjāḥan" with a jīm, then an unpointed ḥāʾ. And mathājij al-māʾ are its outlets.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 15:

﴿That We may bring forth thereby﴾ — i.e., by that water, and it is on its outward meaning according to the early generation (al-salaf) and those who follow them. The Ash'aris said: i.e., with Him (ʿindahu) — ﴿grain and vegetation﴾: that which is eaten as food, such as wheat and barley, and that which is fed to animals, such as herbage and chaff. The mention of grain before vegetation, although vegetation comes before it in the act of bringing forth, is because grain is more fundamental (asalah) and nobler, since most of it is the sustenance of humankind.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 16:

﴿وجَنّاتٍ﴾ (and gardens) is the plural of jannah, which is every orchard with trees whose branches screen the ground from view; the word derives from janna, meaning to conceal, or screen. Al-Farra' said: the jannah is that which contains palm trees, and al-Firdaws is that which contains vines; trees that provide shade may also be called jannah, and the verse of Zuhayr is interpreted accordingly:

مِنَ النَّواضِحِ تَسْقِي جَنَّةً سُحُقًا

("from the water-carrying camels that irrigate a jannah of tall, distant palms")

and this is the meaning intended here. As for the Exalted One's words ﴿ألْفافًا﴾ (dense), it means intertwined, with some of them overlapping others. It was said: it has no singular, like awza' and akhyaf for scattered, differing groups. This is the view chosen by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Qutayba said: it is the plural of luff, with the lam vowelled with a damma, which is the plural of laffa', so it is a plural of a plural. This was considered unlikely, since no parallel of this pattern occurs: khudr is the plural of khadra', and humr is the plural of hamra', but akhdar is not a plural of khudr, nor ahmar a plural of humr; and the plural of a plural is not regular. The existence of a parallel in isolated words is not sufficient, so it is said.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is the plural of lafif, meaning malfuf (wrapped together), and fa'il is pluralized on the pattern af'al, like sharif and ashraf. The grammarians differed only over whether it is a plural of fa'il. In al-Kashshaf: "If it were said that it is the plural of multaffa, with the deletion of the extra letters, that would be a plausible statement," and the quotation ends there. The deletion of extra letters is what grammarians call tarkhim (apocope) in such cases, because the regular plural of multaffa is multaffat, not alfaf. Al-Kashshaf's critic in al-Kashf objected to this, saying: it has no parallel, because the apocopated diminutive is established, but its plural is not. It has been said, however, that this is not accepted, for it occurs in their speech and they did not address it because of its rarity. The truth is that it is a strained view. Most lexicographers hold that it is the plural of liff with a kasra, an adjectival form (sifa mushabbaha) meaning malfuf, and fi'l is pluralized on the pattern af'al regularly, like jidh and ajdha'. From the author of al-Iqlid, it is related that he said: al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Tusi recited to me:

جَنَّةٌ لِفٌّ وعَيْشٌ مُغْدِقٌ ونُدامى كُلُّهم بِيضٌ زُهُرْ

("a garden dense with growth, a life of abundance, and companions all of them fair and bright")

Al-Qamus allowed that it may be the plural of laff with a fatha, this being so. And in what has been mentioned of the Exalted One's acts is evidence for the soundness and truth of resurrection from three aspects, as has been said. The first is in regard to His power, Mighty and Majestic: whoever is able to bring into being those wondrous things without a model to imitate or a law to follow is more able and more powerful to bring about return.

The second is in regard to His knowledge and wisdom: whoever has originated these created things in a marvelous pattern, leading to glorious ends and beautiful benefits returning to creation, it would be impossible in wisdom for him not to make for them an outcome.

The third is in regard to the act itself: waking after sleep is a model of resurrection after death, which everyone witnesses, and likewise the bringing forth of grain and plants from the earth is seen at every moment. It is as if it were said: We have done, or have We not done, these outward acts that point, in manifold ways, to the truth of resurrection, which necessitates belief in it? So why do you plunge into it in denial, and ask about it in mockery?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Judgment is an appointed time﴾ begins the explanation of the secret behind delaying that about which they ask and seek to hasten, saying: ("When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?")
Page 12
It is also a kind of detail about how it will occur and what they will meet then of the various kinds of punishment, in accordance with what the threat had already described in summary. Some of the eminent scholars said: when He, glorified be He, established the truth of resurrection, it was the place where one would naturally ask about its time, so it was said: ("Indeed") and so on. It was emphasized because it is among the things they doubted, and it is not so. That is, indeed the Day of the Separation (fasl) of Allah, exalted is His majesty, among the creatures was, in His knowledge, mighty and majestic, an appointed time and a fixed term for the resurrection of the first and the last and for what follows from it of recompense, reward and punishment, which will not be transgressed by being brought forward or delayed. It was also said: it is a limit by which the world is timed and at which it ends, or a limit for the creatures at which they come to an end so that their states may be distinguished. The first is more suited to the context, since the world ends, as it is said, at the first blast. Whatever the case, the past tense in "kāna" is considered with respect to knowledge. It is also permitted that it means "yakūn" (will be), and the future is expressed in the past tense to indicate the certainty of its occurrence.

﴿يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ في الصُّورِ﴾ أي النفخةَ الثانيةَ. (*Yawma*) بدلٌ من ﴿يَوْمَ الفَصْلِ﴾ (*badal*, substitute) أو عطفُ بيانٍ (*'atf bayan*, explicative apposition) مفيدٌ لزيادةِ تفخيمِه وتهويلِه. ولا ضَيْرَ في تأخُّرِ الفصلِ عن النفخِ، فإنه زمانٌ ممتدٌّ يقعُ في مبدئه النفخُ، وفي بقيَّتِه الفصلُ ومبادئُه وآثارُه. وتقدَّم الكلامُ في *الصور* (*al-Sur*, the Trumpet). وقرأ أبو عِياضٍ: «فِي الصَّوَرِ» بفتحِ الواوِ، جمعَ *صورة*، وقد مرَّ الكلامُ في ذلك أيضًا.

والفاءُ في قولِه تعالى: ﴿فَتَأْتُونَ﴾ فصيحةٌ (*fa-faṣīḥa*, the fa that expresses an omitted clause)، تُفصِحُ عن جملةٍ قد حُذِفَتْ ثقةً بدلالةِ الحالِ عليها، وإيذانًا بغايةِ سرعةِ الإتيانِ، كما في قولِه تعالى: ﴿أنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصاكَ البَحْرَ فانْفَلَقَ﴾. أي: فتحيَوْنَ فتُبْعَثونَ من قبوركم فتأتونَ إلى الموقفِ عَقِيبَ ذلك من غيرِ لُبْثٍ أصلًا.

﴿أفْواجًا﴾ أي: أُمَمًا، كلُّ أمةٍ بإمامِها، كما قال سبحانه: ﴿يَوْمَ نَدْعُوا كُلَّ أُناسٍ بِإمامِهِمْ﴾. أو زُمَرًا وجماعاتٍ مختلفةَ الأحوالِ متباينةَ الأوضاعِ حسبَ اختلافِ الأعمالِ وتباينِها.

واستُدِلَّ لهذا بما خرَّجَ ابنُ مردويه عن البراءِ بنِ عازبٍ: «أنَّ مُعاذَ بنَ جبلٍ قال: يا رسولَ اللهِ، ما قولُ اللهِ تعالى: ﴿يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ في الصُّورِ فَتَأْتُونَ أفْواجًا﴾؟ فقال: "يا مُعاذُ، سألتَ عن عظيمٍ من الأمورِ". ثم أرسلَ عينيْه، ثم قال عليه الصلاةُ والسلامُ: "عشرةُ أصنافٍ قد ميَّزَهم عزَّ وجلَّ من جماعةِ المسلمينَ فبدَّلَ صُوَرَهم، فبعضُهم على صورةِ القِرَدةِ، وبعضُهم على صورةِ الخنازيرِ، وبعضُهم منكَّسينَ أرجلُهم فوقُ، وجوهُهم أسفلُ يُسْحَبونَ عليها، وبعضُهم عميٌ يتردَّدونَ، وبعضُهم صمٌّ بكمٌ لا يعقلونَ، وبعضُهم يمضغونَ ألسنتَهم وهي مدلاةٌ على صدورِهم يسيلُ القيحُ من أفواهِهم لعابًا يتقذَّرُهم أهلُ الجمعِ، وبعضُهم مقطَّعةٌ أيديهم وأرجلُهم، وبعضُهم مصلَّبونَ على جذوعٍ من نارٍ، وبعضُهم أشدُّ نتنًا من الجيفِ، وبعضُهم مُلْبَسونَ جِبابًا سابغةً من قطرانٍ لازقةً بجلودِهم. فأمَّا الذينَ على صورةِ القِرَدةِ فالقتَّاتُ من الناسِ، وأمَّا الذينَ على صورةِ الخنازيرِ فأكلةُ السُّحتِ، وأمَّا المنكَّسونَ على وجوهِهم فأكلةُ الرِّبا، وأمَّا العميُ فالذينَ يجورونَ في الحكمِ، وأمَّا الصمُّ البكمُ فالمعجبونَ بأعمالِهم، وأمَّا الذينَ يمضغونَ ألسنتَهم فالعلماءُ والقصَّاصُ الذينَ خالفَ أقوالَهم أعمالُهم، وأمَّا الذينَ قُطِّعتْ أيديهم وأرجلُهم فهم الذينَ يؤذونَ الجيرانَ، وأمَّا المصلَّبونَ على جذوعٍ من نارٍ فالساعونَ بالناسِ إلى السلطانِ، وأمَّا الذينَ هم أشدُّ نتنًا من الجيفِ فالذينَ يتمتَّعونَ بالشهواتِ واللذَّاتِ ويمنعونَ حقَّ اللهِ تعالى من أموالِهم، وأمَّا الذينَ يلبسونَ الجِبابَ فأهلُ الكِبرِ والخُيلاءِ والفخرِ".»

وهذا كما قال ابنُ حجرٍ: حديثٌ موضوعٌ، وآثارُ الوضعِ لائحةٌ عليه. وعليه قيل: لا بدَّ من التغليبِ (*taghlib*, the figure of speech where the masculine plural covers mixed groups) في قولِه تعالى: (تَأْتُونَ)؛ إذ لا يمكنُ الإتيانُ للمصلوبِ والمسحوبِ على الوجهِ، ولا لمن قُطِّعتْ يداهُ ورجلاهُ. وتُعُقِّبَ بأنه ليس بشيءٍ؛ فإنَّ أمورَ الآخرةِ لا تُقاسُ على أمورِ الدنيا، والقادرُ على البعثِ قادرٌ على جعلِهم ماشينَ بلا أيدٍ وأرجلٍ، وأن تمشيَ بهم عُمَدُ النارِ التي صُلِبوا عليها، مع أنه لا يلزمُ أن يأتوا بأنفسِهم لجوازِ أن تأتيَ بهم الزبانيةُ (*al-Zabaniyah*, the angels of punishment).

﴿And the heaven will be opened﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿will be blown﴾ according to what has been said. The use of the past form (ṣīghat al-māḍī) indicates certainty. It is related from al-Zamakhsharī that it is coordinated with ﴿then you will come﴾. It is not a condition that the two verbs agree in time, as one who is not a grammarian supposes. al-Ṭībī, in *al-Kashf*, approved this and said: "The condition for its goodness is that it be close to the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), or that the present tense be a narration of a past state. What we are dealing with is a present-tense verb expressed in the past form, to magnify it and to affirm the certainty of its occurrence, so it is closer to being near to it." If it were made a circumstantial clause, meaning ﴿then you will come while the heaven has been opened﴾, that would be a valid view.

The majority of readers, that is, all except the Kufans, read ﴿futtiḥat﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdīd). It has been said that this is the more fitting reading, in view of the Exalted's words: ﴿so it became gates﴾. The opening (fatḥ) has been interpreted as splitting (shaqq), in view of the Exalted's words: ﴿when the heaven splits asunder﴾ and His words: ﴿when the heaven bursts apart﴾, and so on. The Qur'an explains one part of itself by another. The sense of opening in this meaning occurs as in "the opening of the bridges" and what resembles it. Perhaps the reason for expressing it by this is to indicate the perfection of His power, so that the splitting of this great body is like opening a door in ease and speed. The meaning of "became" (ṣāra) is intended, and the verb indicates the transition from one state to another. As for the fact that a sky split apart does not literally become gates, they said: the speech is based on an eloquent simile (tashbīh balīgh), that is: its splits became, because of their width, like gates; or, because of the multitude of splits, it is as if the whole were gates; or it is by way of an elided genitive construction (taqdīr muḍāf), that is: it became possessed of gates.

It has been said: the opening is on its literal sense, with the speech employing an elided genitive construction referring to the heaven, that is: the gates of the heaven were opened, so it became as if all of it were gates. This agrees with its being split, so it is split and its gates are opened. It has been objected that its splitting is for the descent of the angels, as the Exalted said: ﴿and on the day the heaven is split open with the clouds, and the angels are sent down in descent﴾. So when it is split, there is no need for opening its gates. Also, the opening of its gates is not among the special features of the Day of Judgment. There is discussion on this. Yes, the first interpretation is preferable.

It has been said that the meaning is opening the place of the heaven by removal (kashṭ), so that all of it becomes paths that nothing blocks. This is far-fetched.

On what has preceded in this verse there is a refutation of those who claim the impossibility of rending the heaven. And on this interpretation there is in it a refutation of those who claim its removal (kashṭ), as is well known from the earlier philosophers, although Mulla Sadra (al-Shīrāzī) established in *al-Asfār* that their leading figures held otherwise. The philosophers today deny the heaven known among Muslims, and they have not produced anything to which the verses and the authentic reports concerning its description could be interpreted, as is not hidden from the intelligent and fair-minded person.

**[Verse 20]: "And the mountains will be set in motion."** That is, they will move through the air in their own form after being pulverized and after being uprooted from their places. This is indicated by His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass by like the passing of clouds﴾ [27:88]. Also included in this is the comparison of the mountains to the "clouds" (*hibal al-sahab*, a wordplay on *jibal*, mountains) in the looseness of their parts and their dispersal, as His, the Exalted, saying indicates: ﴿And the mountains will be like tufts of wool, fluffed up﴾ [101:5].

**"So they will become a mirage (*sarab*)."** That is, after being set in motion they will become like a mirage. After their pulverization and their rising into the air, you will see them as if they were mountains, though they are not mountains but a thick, piled-up dust that appears from afar as if it were a mountain, just as the mirage appears as if it were a sea, for example, though there is no water in it. So the statement is a case of eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), and the common quality (*al-jami'*) is that each of the mountains and the mirage appears as something while not being that thing. It is also permitted that the point of resemblance is the looseness of the parts (*takhalkhul*), since after being set in motion they will become scattered dust, as the Exalted said: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to powder﴾ [56:5] ﴿and will become scattered dust﴾ [56:6].

What is derived from *al-Azhar al-Badi'a fi 'Ilm al-Tabi'a* by Muhammad al-Harrawi is that the mirage is air whose lower layer, adjacent to the earth, has been heated, as the earth is heated by the sun's heat, so it became rarefied, and part of it rose to the layers above it, which then became denser than what lies beneath. By this heating, the air departed from its natural position near the earth; and because of the reflection and refraction of light rays in it in a particular manner, explained in the aforementioned book, together with the reflection of the color of the sky, it is mistaken for water. The image of an object appears inverted in it, and there may appear in it floating images such as palaces, pillars, and strange, beautiful dwellings, and moving shapes whose forms change every moment, shifting from their places and then vanishing. These are nothing but images resulting from the reflection of distant visible images, or images superimposed on the layers of air of different densities. Therefore, considering rarefaction alone as the point of resemblance is open to question.

Whatever the case, this takes place after the second blast, at the resurrection of creation. God, Mighty and Majestic, sets the mountains in motion, makes them scattered dust, and levels the earth on that day, as His saying indicates: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾ [20:105] ﴿and leave it a level, smooth plain﴾ [20:106] ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or elevation﴾ [20:107] ﴿On that day they will follow the summoner﴾ [20:108], and His saying: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the heavens as well, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer﴾ [14:48]. The "following" of the summoner, who is Israfil, peace be upon him, and the emergence of creation before God, the Exalted, occur only after the second blast. As for the crumbling and splitting of the mountains, it occurs at the first blast. It has been said that their being set in motion and becoming a mirage also occurs at the first blast, but the apparent meaning of the verse contradicts this. Yes, if the clause were taken as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "Then you will come in throngs while the mountains have been set in motion and have become a mirage," that would be possible. The apparent meaning is that they become a mirage for the leveling of the earth, and it is not far-fetched that there are other wisdoms in it. As for the saying of some that they flow like water and stream like it, like a mirage, and that this increases the agitation of those thirsty on the Gathering Day and the intensity of their longing for water, it contradicts the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 21:

﴿Indeed, Hell has been ever lying in wait﴾. This begins the detailing of the rulings of the Judgment Day (al-faṣl) to which "the Day" was just attributed, after the explanation of its terror. Al-Mirṣād (a place of lying in wait) is a noun of place, like al-midmār (the place where horses are trained through lean feeding and exercise), and it takes the pattern mif'āl, which is so as clearly stated by al-Rāghib, al-Jawharī and others. It may also be a noun of instrument, and an intensive adjective. The apparent meaning is that it is a literal sense in all of these: that is, a place of watching and waiting, where the guardians of the Fire lie in wait for the disbelievers in order to punish them. It has been said: the guardians of Paradise lie in wait there for the believers in order to protect them from its heat as they cross over it. It has also been said: the angels, peace be upon them, lie in wait there for both groups, so that one of them punishes the other, namely the believing group, and punishes the other group, namely the disbelieving group. It is also permissible that it be an intensive form, like minḥār (one who slaughters much); that is, one who is diligent in watching the disbelievers so that not one of them escapes; or diligent in watching the believers so that none of them is harmed by its heat; or diligent in watching both groups in the manner you have just heard.

The attribution of this to it is either metaphorical or in the manner of a simile.

In al-Baḥr: "mirṣādan" carries the sense of a relative noun, that is, possessing lying-in-wait (dhāt raṣad). Al-Mirṣād may also be explained as simply "the path," which is one of its meanings, and then it applies to both groups. For this reason al-Ḥasan said, as transmitted from him by Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd regarding the verse: "No one enters Paradise until he crosses over the Fire." Qatādah said, as transmitted from him by the same narrators: "Know that there is no way to Paradise until the Fire is crossed."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 22:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for the tyrants﴾ (lil-tagheen), that is, those who exceed the limit in transgression (al-tughyan). It is connected to an implied element, and it is either an attributive (na't) of ﴿a watching post﴾ (mirsadan), meaning "existing for the tyrants," or a circumstantial clause (hal) of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a place of return﴾ (ma'aban). It was placed before it because the latter is indefinite (nakira); had it been postponed, it would have been an attribute of it. That is: they shall have a place of return and a refuge existing for them, to which they will certainly return and take shelter. It has also been permitted that it be another predicate (khabar) of "they were" (kanat), or that it be connected to "a place of return" (ma'aban) or to "a watching post" (mirsad). Accordingly, it has been said: the meaning of ﴿a watching post﴾ for them is that it is prepared for them, from their saying "arsadtu lahu" (I prepared for him), i.e., I made ready and requited him with good or with evil. As for "a place of return" (ma'aban), it has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for "a watching post" (mirsadan) in all respects, a substitute of whole for whole. It has also been said that it is a second predicate of "they were" (kanat) or an attribute of "a watching post" (mirsad).

And ﴿for the tyrants﴾ (lil-tagheen) is connected to it, or is a circumstantial clause of it, according to some of the earlier interpretations of ﴿they were a watching post﴾ (kanat mirsadan), so reflect carefully. Abu 'Amr, al-Minqari and Ibn Ya'mur recited "anna Jahannama" (that Hell) with a fatha on the hamza, presupposing a preposition lam of causation (lam al-jarr li-ta'lil) for the establishment of the Hour, which is understood from the speech. The meaning is: that was for the establishment of recompense. It has been objected that in that case it should also be "anna lil-muttaqeen" with a fatha and coordinated with what is here, because by both of them the causation through the establishment of recompense is completed. Unless it is said: the conjunction was omitted to indicate that each of the two recompenses independently calls for the establishment of the Hour. But this is open to scrutiny, because by that the recompense is completed; as for the establishment itself, what has been mentioned suffices as its cause. Moreover, if what is meant earlier was "they were a watching post for the two groups," as you have heard, this speech would not be coherent at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 23:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Lābithīna fīhā﴾ (remaining in it), meaning: abiding in Jahannam, staying in it constantly. It is a predicative circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah) from the pronoun in ﴿lil-ṭāghīn﴾ (for the transgressors).

ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd), ʿAlqamah, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Ibn Wathhāb, ʿAmr ibn Sharḥabīl, Ibn Jubayr, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash, Ḥamzah, Qutaybah, Sawrah and Rawḥ recited «Labithīna» without an alif after the lām. In this form there is an intensity (mubālaghah) that is not present in ﴿Lābithīna﴾. Abū Ḥayyān said: the pattern fāʿil indicates one in whom the act has occurred, while the pattern faʿil indicates one whose nature or characteristic it is, like ḥādhir and ḥadhir.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿aḥqāban﴾ (for ages) is a time adverb for their remaining, and so is aḥqub, the plural of ḥuqub, with a single ḍammah or with two ḍammahs. According to what is reported from al-Ḥasan, it means an unspecified period of time, and some lexicographers' explanation of it as "dahr" (an age) is similar. Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr and al-Ḥākim, who declared it authentic, reported from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: one ḥuqub is eighty years. al-Bazzār reported something similar from Abū Hurayrah, and Ibn Jarīr from Ibn ʿAbbās,
