and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn ʿUmar. It is also reported from a group of the early generations (salaf) that each day of it, that is here, is the measure of a thousand years of the years of this world. 

al-Bazzār, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylamī reported from Ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that it is some eighty years, each year three hundred and sixty days, and the day is a thousand years of what you count.

It is also said: forty years. Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit a ḥadīth traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) on this. Some lexicographers said: seventy thousand years. Many have preferred explaining it as "dahr." In any case, the meaning of ﴿Lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾ is: successive, such that whenever one ḥuqub passes, another ḥuqub follows it. The indication of succession comes from usage, as attested by its derivation, for it is from ḥaqībah, which is what is tied behind the rider, and successive things are such that one is behind the other. Thus the verse contains nothing indicating the exit of the disbelievers from the Fire or the absence of their eternity therein, since the sense of succession is understood from usage. The form of paucity (ṣīghat al-qillah) does not contradict infinity, for there is no difference between the succession of many ḥuqub without end and the succession of few ḥuqub in that manner. It is also said: the form here is shared between paucity and abundance, since ḥuqub has no plural of abundance, so it should be taken, by aid of the context, to mean the plural of abundance. This was objected to on the ground that the plural of abundance for it is established, namely ḥuqub, as al-Rāghib mentioned. What I have seen in his Mufradāt is that ḥiqab, that is with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a fatḥah on the qāf, is ḥiqbah, which is explained as eighty years. Yes, it is said: this is contradicted by what has been reported, that "some people of the Fire will be brought out of the Fire and brought near to Paradise, until when they inhale its fragrance and see what Allah has prepared for His believing servants in it, it will be said: turn them away from it, they have no share in it. So they will be returned to the Fire with a regret such that the first and the last have not returned with its like." It was objected that if this is authentic, it contradicts only if the exit were for full ḥuqub; but if it were in part of the ḥuqub, there is no contradiction, since the succession of the ḥuqub as a whole remains. Granting that, this exit which entails return is for increased punishment, and remaining in the Fire is more severe; and the speech is by way of dominance (taghlīb), and there is in it no combining of literal and figurative meaning. Then, even if it is found that the verse indicates termination and exit from the Fire, even after a long time, that is an implicit meaning opposed by the explicit clear text to the contrary, like the verses of eternity, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa mā hum bikhārijīna minhā wa lahum ʿadhābun muqīm﴾ (They will never leave it, and for them is a lasting punishment), and so on. And if His saying, Exalted is He, is taken as...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 24–25:

﴿They shall not taste therein any coolness, nor any drink,﴾ ﴿except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid.﴾ [This is] a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in ﴿lābithīna﴾ (remaining). It then serves as a restriction on the lingering (labth), so it is possible that they remain therein for ages (aḥqāban), not tasting [anything] except boiling water and ghassāq. Then, after the ages, there will be for them a lingering in another state of punishment. Likewise, if ﴿aḥqāban﴾ is taken as the object of ﴿lā yadhūqūna﴾ and this is a restriction on it, though it is remote. The same applies if ﴿lā yadhūqūna fīhā﴾ and so on is taken as a description of ﴿aḥqāban﴾, with the pronoun (fīhā) referring to them (the ages) and not to Jahannam; but this is more remote than the previous [view]. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the tāghūn" (transgressors) is that which stands opposite to "the muttaqūn" (the God-fearing), so it includes the sinners, and the [eternal] end (tanāhī) is considered with regard to the whole; and this, as you see, [is weak].

As for the statement of Muqātil that this is abrogated by the verse ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾, it is false, as is not hidden. It is also permitted that ﴿aḥqāban﴾ is the plural of ḥiqb, like ḥadhir, from "ḥaqiba al-rajul" when sustenance eluded him, and "ḥaqiba al-ʿām" when its rain and goodness became scarce; the meaning being: deprived of pleasure, which is a metaphor for their being punished. Then it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿lābithīna﴾.

The statement of Allah the Exalted ﴿lā yadhūqūna﴾ is either a clarifying description or an explanatory sentence with no place in terms of i'rāb. According to what was mentioned first, it is an independent sentence serving as a predicate about them. The meaning of "al-bard" (coolness) is that which refreshes them and relieves them from the heat of the Fire; this does not contradict that they may be punished with the zamharīr (bitter cold). "Al-sharāb" (drink) is well known. "Al-ḥamīm" is water of intense heat, and "al-ghassāq" is what drips from the skins of the people of the Fire of pus; that is: they shall not taste therein anything at all, neither any breath that relieves them from the heat of the Fire, nor any drink that quenches their thirst, but they shall taste boiling water and pus.

In a hadith: "Indeed, when one of them brings that near his mouth, the skin of his face falls off, until only bones remain, rattling."

From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "al-bard" is cold drink that is pleasant. From this is the statement of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:

They are given to drink from the rosy wine of al-Barīṣ, a coolness that is mixed with pure sealed wine.

And the statement of another:

Sweet promises from Suʿdā, as if Suʿdā had given you to drink from them, when you were thirsty, a cold drink.

So ﴿nor any drink﴾ is a general negation after a specific one. Abū ʿUbayda, al-Kisāʾī, al-Faḍl ibn Khālid and Muʿādh al-Naḥwī said: "al-bard" is sleep, and the Arabs call it that because it cools the heat of thirst; and from their speech: "al-bard prevented [him]." The poet said:

Had you wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and had you wished, I would not have tasted sweet water nor cold sleep.

That is, it is a metaphor for that according to some. Al-Baḥr reports from the book "al-Lughāt fī al-Qur'ān" that "al-bard" is sleep in the dialect of Hudhayl. From Ibn ʿAbbas and Abū al-ʿĀliya: "al-ghassāq" is the zamharīr. This, as has been said, is an exception from ﴿bardan﴾, but it was placed later to match the endings of the verses, so do not be heedless.

Several of the seven readers read "ghasāqan" with light (unstressed) pronunciation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 24–25:

﴿They shall not taste therein any coolness, nor any drink,﴾ ﴿except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid.﴾ [This is] a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in ﴿lābithīna﴾ (remaining). It then serves as a restriction on the lingering (labth), so it is possible that they remain therein for ages (aḥqāban), not tasting [anything] except boiling water and ghassāq. Then, after the ages, there will be for them a lingering in another state of punishment. Likewise, if ﴿aḥqāban﴾ is taken as the object of ﴿lā yadhūqūna﴾ and this is a restriction on it, though it is remote. The same applies if ﴿lā yadhūqūna fīhā﴾ and so on is taken as a description of ﴿aḥqāban﴾, with the pronoun (fīhā) referring to them (the ages) and not to Jahannam; but this is more remote than the previous [view]. It has been said: the intended meaning of "the tāghūn" (transgressors) is that which stands opposite to "the muttaqūn" (the God-fearing), so it includes the sinners, and the [eternal] end (tanāhī) is considered with regard to the whole; and this, as you see, [is weak].

As for the statement of Muqātil that this is abrogated by the verse ﴿So taste, for We shall not increase you except in punishment﴾, it is false, as is not hidden. It is also permitted that ﴿aḥqāban﴾ is the plural of ḥiqb, like ḥadhir, from "ḥaqiba al-rajul" when sustenance eluded him, and "ḥaqiba al-ʿām" when its rain and goodness became scarce; the meaning being: deprived of pleasure, which is a metaphor for their being punished. Then it is a ḥāl from the pronoun in ﴿lābithīna﴾.

The statement of Allah the Exalted ﴿lā yadhūqūna﴾ is either a clarifying description or an explanatory sentence with no place in terms of i'rāb. According to what was mentioned first, it is an independent sentence serving as a predicate about them. The meaning of "al-bard" (coolness) is that which refreshes them and relieves them from the heat of the Fire; this does not contradict that they may be punished with the zamharīr (bitter cold). "Al-sharāb" (drink) is well known. "Al-ḥamīm" is water of intense heat, and "al-ghassāq" is what drips from the skins of the people of the Fire of pus; that is: they shall not taste therein anything at all, neither any breath that relieves them from the heat of the Fire, nor any drink that quenches their thirst, but they shall taste boiling water and pus.

In a hadith: "Indeed, when one of them brings that near his mouth, the skin of his face falls off, until only bones remain, rattling."

From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "al-bard" is cold drink that is pleasant. From this is the statement of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:

They are given to drink from the rosy wine of al-Barīṣ, a coolness that is mixed with pure sealed wine.

And the statement of another:

Sweet promises from Suʿdā, as if Suʿdā had given you to drink from them, when you were thirsty, a cold drink.

So ﴿nor any drink﴾ is a general negation after a specific one. Abū ʿUbayda, al-Kisāʾī, al-Faḍl ibn Khālid and Muʿādh al-Naḥwī said: "al-bard" is sleep, and the Arabs call it that because it cools the heat of thirst; and from their speech: "al-bard prevented [him]." The poet said:

Had you wished, I would have forbidden women other than you, and had you wished, I would not have tasted sweet water nor cold sleep.

That is, it is a metaphor for that according to some. Al-Baḥr reports from the book "al-Lughāt fī al-Qur'ān" that "al-bard" is sleep in the dialect of Hudhayl. From Ibn ʿAbbas and Abū al-ʿĀliya: "al-ghassāq" is the zamharīr. This, as has been said, is an exception from ﴿bardan﴾, but it was placed later to match the endings of the verses, so do not be heedless.

"Recompense" (jaza'an): i.e., "Be recompensed with that as recompense." Here (jaza'an) is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) in the accusative, governed by a verb understood (muqaddar). To make it another predicate for "kanat" (laysa bi-shay' — "they were not"), would be of no value.

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿wifaqan﴾ (in accordance), are a verbal noun (masdar) from "wafaqahu," and it is an attribute of it (the recompense) with an omitted noun understood: that is, "possessing correspondence," or by interpreting it as an active participle (ism al-fa'il), or for the purpose of emphasis (mubalaghah), as is known in such cases. In any case, what is meant is a recompense corresponding to their deeds, in the sense that it is equal to them in severity and lightness according to what they deserve, as His justice and wisdom, exalted is He, require. The clause formed from the understood verb and its complement is a circumstantial clause (hal) or a resumptive independent clause (mustanaffah). It is also permitted that ﴿wifaqan﴾ be a masdar in the accusative governed by an understood verb as well, meaning "it corresponded to them in correspondence," and this clause would then be in the position of an attribute of "jaza'an."

Al-Farra' said: it is the plural of "wifq," and the difficulty of making it an attribute of "jaza'an" in that case is not hidden. Abu Haywa, Abu Bahriyya and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wiffaqan" with a kasra on the waw and a shadda on the fa', from "wafaqahu yafiquhu," like "warithahu yarithuhu," meaning he found it corresponding to his condition. In al-Kashf: "wafaqahu" has the sense of "wafaqahu" (corresponded to him), and describing the recompense with it is not a description of its possessor's state, as is not hidden. Ibn al-Qutiyya related: "wafaqa amruhu," meaning it was good; but this meaning is not what is intended here.

Verse 27 says: ﴿Indeed, they used not to hope for a reckoning﴾. This is a justification for the punishment mentioned (earlier), meaning: they used not to fear that they would be called to account for their deeds.

﴿And they denied Our signs﴾, those that bear witness to this, or to it and to other matters that must be believed in, ﴿with [great] denial﴾. That is, an excessive denial. The form *fi‘āl* (فِعّالٌ), used here as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun) with the meaning of *tafʿīl* (the second form), is a regular and common pattern in the speech of the eloquent Arabs. It is reported from al-Farrāʾ that it is a fluent Yemeni dialect. An Arab Bedouin, on the hill of al-Marwah, once asked me for a ruling: "Is the shaving (*al-ḥalq*) more beloved to you, or the shortening (*al-qiṣṣār*)?" From this dialect is the saying of the poet:

"How long has it kept me from my companions, and from a need whose fulfilment is from my recovery."

Ibn Mālik said in *al-Tashīl* that it is rare. And ʿAlī, may God honour his face, ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī, Abū Rajāʾ, al-Aʿmash and ʿĪsā, according to one report from him, read it with the lightened form. The author of *al-Lawāmiḥ* said: "That is the dialect of Yemen; they make the verbal noun of *kadhaba* light, *kidhāban*, like *kataba*, *kitāban*, so *kidhāban* means *kadhiban* (lying)." On this is the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"So I believed her, and I disbelieved her, and a man benefits from his lying."

The expression here is, according to this reading, of the type of ﴿He caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ (71:17). Its triliteral verb is either assumed, meaning "they denied Our signs and they denied with denial", or it is a *maṣdar* of the mentioned verb taken as including the meaning of the triliteral *kadhaba* (to lie), since their denial of the plain truth entails that they are liars. In either case it indicates their lying in their denial. It is also permitted that it means *mukādhabah* (mutual denial), like *qitāl* meaning *muqātalah* (mutual fighting). In that case it belongs to the *mufāʿalah* form (the third form, denoting reciprocity), with the sense that each of them, and each of the Muslims, held the other to be lying, the abandonment of belief being treated as an action. It does not mean that each actually denied the other. It is also permitted that the *mufāʿalah* is a metonymy (*majāz mursal*) by the relation of necessity, meaning earnestness and striving in the act. It may also be a metaphor (*istiʿārah*), since they were exaggerating in lying, as those who strive to overcome one another in it. On both meanings, whether it means lying or mutual denial, it is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning "lying" or "denying one another", depending on whether participation is considered or not.

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and al-Mājashūn read *kuḏḏāban* with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf* and a *shaddah* on the *dhāl*. It is interpreted as the plural of *kādhib* (liar), like *fussāq*, the plural of *fāsiq* (sinner). It is then also a circumstantial clause, and the meaning is: "they lied while in the state of their lying", like the case of ﴿when it comes, when it comes﴾ according to what is said about the verse of Ṭarafah:

"When what cannot be avoided comes, then welcome to it, when it comes, without lying or excuses."

There is clear discussion about this, and it is also permitted that it be a single word in the intensive form (*ṣīghat mubālaghah*), like *kubbār* and *ḥassān*, so that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, that is, "a denial, a lying denial". It then indicates exaggeration and the excess of lying, because it is like *laylun ailad* (a very dark night) and *ẓalāmun muẓlim* (intense darkness). The attribution in it is metaphorical.

[Page 17]

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 78, verse 29]**

﴿وكُلَّ شَيْءٍ﴾ (wa-kulla shay'in, "and everything") means: of the things that are among the total of which are their deeds. Abu Hayyan said: that is, everything that is subject to reward and punishment. It is general but specified (ʿāmm makhsūs), and its being in the accusative is by a hidden verb (muḍmar) that is explained by ﴿أحْصَيْناهُ﴾ (aḥṣaynāhu, "We have enumerated it"), meaning: We have preserved it and kept account of it. Abu al-Sammal recited it in the nominative (bi-l-rafʿ) as a beginning (ʿalā al-ibtidāʾ).

﴿كِتابًا﴾ (kitāban, "as a writing") is a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing ﴿أحْصَيْناهُ﴾, since enumeration (iḥṣāʾ) and writing (kutub) share the meaning of preservation (ḍabṭ). Either ﴿أحْصَيْناهُ﴾ is interpreted as "We wrote it" (katabnāhu), or ﴿كِتابًا﴾ is interpreted as "enumeration" (bi-iḥṣāʾin). It is also permitted to treat it as iḥtibāk (interlocking elision) with the two elisions from both ends, or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) meaning "written" (maktūban) in the Preserved Tablet or in the scrolls of the recording angels. The apparent meaning is that the statement is literal. Some of them said: the apparent meaning is that it is an analogy (tamthīl) for the image of the preservation of things in His knowledge, exalted is He, by the preservation of one who enumerates, diligent and precise in preserving by writing. Otherwise, He, mighty and majestic, is free of need for preservation by writing, and this analogy is for our understanding; otherwise, the fixedness (infiḍāb) in His knowledge, exalted is He, is greater and loftier than that it be likened to anything. The well-known position of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) is what we have put forward before, and that is not due to need, but is for a wisdom which the intellects fall short of grasping. The sentence is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ) to affirm the preceding threat, that this is certainly to come and will certainly befall them, because their disobediences are recorded and written, by which they will be confronted on the Day of Recompense. It was said: it is to affirm their disbelief and denial of the signs, that these two are preserved for the recompense; but that is not the case. Some said: "In my view the most correct is that ‘kulla shay’in’ is in the accusative by coordination (ʿaṭf) upon the noun of inna in ﴿إنَّهم كانُوا لا يَرْجُونَ حِسابًا﴾ (innahum kānū lā yarjūna ḥisāban, "indeed they did not expect a reckoning"), and ﴿أحْصَيْناهُ كِتابًا﴾ is a coordination upon its predicate; and the nominative is by coordination upon the position (maḥall) of the noun of inna. The sentences are an explanation that the recompense mentioned is in accordance with their deeds, because a fitting recompense occurs only when actions that necessitate it proceed from them, and their preservation and the non-escape of them from the one who recompenses. So the first two sentences serve to convey the proceeding of the necessitating cause, which is disbelief, expressed by not expecting the reckoning and denying the signs, since that is like knowledge in it; and the last serves to convey the preservation and non-escape; that is, with an incorporation (idmāj) of an indication to the remaining disobediences within it, and it is not a parenthetical clause." End of quotation. What is in it of artificiality (takallluf) is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 78, verse 30:

﴿So taste; for We shall increase you only in punishment.﴾ This is a consequence of their disbelief in the Reckoning and their denial of the signs, and the causal link between the tasting and the command to taste is entirely evident. It has been said: "The more apparent view is that it is connected to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness﴾, etc.; that is, when they have tasted the boiling water (al-hamim) and the dark liquid (al-ghassaq), it will be said to them: ﴿So taste; for We shall increase you﴾, etc. In that case the sentences between the two are parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah)." In this there is the following: it is extremely remote, along with the great amount of parenthetical insertion it involves. It also comes in the form of iltifat (a shift in grammatical address), for emphasis, since it presents them as being brought forward at the time of the command so that they may be addressed with reproach and rebuke, and this is greater in humiliation and belittlement. Had the verb of saying been supposed here, there would be no iltifat.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Hasan who said: "I asked Abu Barzah al-Aslami about the most severe verse in the Book of Allah, exalted is He, against the people of the Fire, and he said: the statement of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So taste; for We shall increase you only in punishment.﴾"

The reason it is the most severe, as has been said, is that it is a reproach on the Day of Judgment, an expression of wrath from the Most Merciful of the merciful, and a cutting off of hope for them, together with what is in *lan* (لَنْ), that is, according to the view that it indicates perpetuity (al-ta'bid): that the cessation of increase is like an impossibility that does not fall within the realm of what is valid.

It has also been said: it is possible that what is meant is that it is the strongest of the Qur'an's arguments against the people of the Fire, for when this threat reached them in the world and they did not fear it, they had accepted eternal punishment in exchange for disbelief, so they have no excuse on the Day of Resurrection in the judgment against them of abiding forever in the Fire. In this there is what there is of remoteness.

The matter of the increase of punishment has been raised as a problem, since it conflicts with the punishment being proportionate to their deeds. It has been answered that it is for preserving the principle, for without it they would have grown accustomed to the punishment that befell them the first time and would not have felt pain from it. This, as you see, is [unconvincing].

It has also been said: since the punishment was for disbelief and sins, and these increase in ugliness at every moment, disbelief at a later time is uglier than it was at an earlier time, and so on. Allah, exalted is He, knew of them, due to the badness of their predisposition, that they would persist in that, and this required an increase in the punishment and its intensity day after day.

It has also been said: since their disbelief was the greatest disbelief, it required the most severe punishment, and the punishment added day after day is among the most severe punishment. And other things have been said. So let it be considered.

[Page 18]

Surah 78, verse 31: "Indeed, for the righteous is a place of triumph."

This begins an account of the excellent conditions of the believers, following the account of the bad conditions of the disbelievers. "Mafazan" (مفازا) is either a mimi verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī) or a noun of place (ism makan). That is, indeed for those who guard against the deeds of disbelief there is triumph and success through their striving, or a place of success. It was also said: deliverance from what those [disbelievers] are in, or a place of deliverance.

Al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*):

﴿حَدائِقَ﴾ is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion, a type of apposition in which the substitute is part of a broader whole or contains what it refers to) for ﴿مَفازًا﴾ according to the first view, and a *badal al-ba'd* (partitive substitute, where the substitute is a part of the thing replaced) according to the second. The connecting pronoun (*al-rabit*) is implied, and its estimated form is: «حَدائِقُ فِيهِ» ("gardens in it"), or «هي في مَحَلِّهِ» ("they are in its place"), or something similar.

It is also permitted that it be a *badal al-kull* (total substitute, where the substitute is the whole of what it replaces), on the basis of *al-idda'* (assumption or treating it as such). Or it may be in the accusative with an implied verb «أعْنِي» ("I mean"). «حَدائِقَ» is the plural of «حَدِيقَةٍ», meaning an orchard containing kinds of fruit-bearing trees. Some scholars added: and fragrant plants and flowers. Al-Raghib said: it is a piece of land that has water, and it was so named by likeness to the pupil of the eye, in its shape and in water being present in it. It seems he meant: a place with water and trees.

﴿وأعْنابًا﴾ is the plural of «عِنَبٍ». The word is also used for the vine itself and for its fruit. The more immediate reading is that it is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to «حَدائِقَ» before it. In that case it is part of the gardens, if what is meant by it is the vines, while the gardens include the trees and their place. It is singled out for mention out of special concern for it. If, however, what is meant is the vines alone with the place, then this does not hold. The *ishtimal* reading is required if what is meant is the fruit of the vines. It is also permitted that it, and likewise what follows it, be conjoined to «مَفازًا».

**"And maidens with full, rounded breasts"**: plural of *kā'ib*, which refers to a woman whose breasts have become firm and rounded, rising slightly, and this occurs at the age of puberty and in the best of proportion.

**"Of equal age"** (*atrāban*): that is, companions of the same age who grow up together, the comparison being in equality and similarity with the *tarā'ib* (the ribs of the chest). Or it is because they are all gathered together upon the *turāb* (dust), that is, the earth. And in some exegeses it is said: all the women of Paradise are maidens of sixteen years, and their men are sons of thirty-three.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 34:

﴿And a cup overflowing.﴾ That is: brimming full (mutraʿah). It is said: Fulan daqqa al-hawd and adhqahu, meaning he filled it (malaʾahu). It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he explained it with this meaning, and he recited the verse of the poet:

"ʿAmir came to us seeking our hospitality, so we filled for him a cup overflowing (dihaqan)."

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): ad-dihaq means "full," derived from ad-dahq, which is pressing and tightening a thing with the hand, as if it was pressed together by its fullness. It is related from Mujahid and a group that its meaning is "successive" (mutatabiʿah). Al-Hakim authenticated from Ibn ʿAbbas what many have narrated, that he said: it is "full, brimming, and successive." I have perhaps heard al-ʿAbbas say: "O boy, give us to drink and fill (adhiq) for us." Ibn Jarir related from ʿIkrimah that he said: that is, pure, though it is not free of turbidity. The majority hold the first view.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 35:

﴿They do not hear therein﴾, i.e., in Paradise. It is also said: in the cup. The fa' (fa', "so/therefore") is taken to indicate causation (sababiyyah). ﴿Idle talk﴾ (laghw) is speech that is not considered of any worth, and it is, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, that which is uttered without deliberation or thought, and so it is treated like the babbling (al-lughā) of birds, namely the sound of sparrows and similar birds. Every ugly speech may also be called laghw, and likewise whatever is of no account in any sense.

﴿Nor lying﴾ (kidhdhaban), i.e., denial (takdhiban). It has also been read with a light pronunciation, so that it means kidhaban or mukadhabah (mutual lying). These mentioned things include kinds of sensory pleasure, as is not hidden.

﴿A reward from your Lord﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid), in the accusative, with the meaning that for the God-fearing there is an achievement (mafāzan). It is as if it were said: He rewarded the God-fearing with "mafāzan" as a reward that comes from your Lord. The mention of the title of Lordship (rubūbiyyah) indicates that this came about through His arrangement and guidance, may He be exalted. The attribution of "Lord" to the Prophet's pronoun, peace be upon him, and not to them, is to honour him, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace. It has been said: He did not say "from their Lord" lest the polytheists take it to refer to their idols, but this is very far-fetched. What we have mentioned makes clear the reason for omitting "from your Lord" in His previous words, ﴿a reward in full measure﴾, and for the absence there of attributing the reward to Him under another title. It has been said that this is in the manner of the saying: "O Allah, indeed good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You."

His words, ﴿a gift﴾, mean: by way of bounty and kindness from Him, mighty and majestic, since nothing is obligatory upon Him, glorified is He. It is a substitute (badal) for "reward." The meaning of it being a reward is that it is so by the necessity of His promise, majestic and exalted is He.

It is permissible that it be in the accusative governed by "reward" (jazā'an), functioning as a direct object. Abu Ḥayyān objected to this, saying that "reward" is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence, and an emphatic verbal noun does not govern, without any disagreement, because it is known to the grammarians that it cannot be resolved into a verb and a verbal particle. This was rebutted: that applies when the verb governing the absolute object is mentioned; but if it is omitted entirely, there is a disagreement as to whether it is the agent of the omitted verb or the verb itself. Al-Shihāb said:

The truth is what Abu Ḥayyān said, because what is mentioned here is the emphatic verbal noun that emphasises itself or something else, whereas what the grammarians disagree about is the verbal noun that comes as a substitute for the verb's own word, as in the line:

"Like Zurayq of wealth squandering it like the foxes."

And his saying:

"O You who accept repentance, forgiving sins, for which I have already been guilty, and I am fearful and trembling because of them."

So let this be understood.

His words, ﴿reckoning﴾, are an adjective of "gift," meaning sufficient, on the basis that it is a verbal noun placed in the position of an adjective, or that it is exaggerated in this respect, or that it is on the assumption of an omitted noun. It is derived from the saying of people: "aḥsabahu al-shay'," when it suffices him, until one says "ḥasbī" (enough for me). It has also been said: "according to their deeds," that is, distributed in proportion to them. This was narrated from Mujāhid. It seems that the intended meaning is distributed after the multiplication, according to that, and thus the objection that it is unsuitable for the multiplication of good deeds is dispelled. For this reason he did not say "in full measure," as in the earlier verse. It is also rebutted by saying that this is an explanation of what is the basic principle, not of the reward in general. It has also been said: the meaning is a gift that is not reckoned against them, unlike the blessings of this world. This has been objected to on the grounds that it is far from the wording, together with what it entails of ambiguity.

Ibn Quṭayb read ﴿ḥassāban﴾ with a fatḥah on the ḥā' and a shaddah on the sīn. Ibn Jinnī said: he formed it as fi'āl from af'ala, like dirāk from adraka, so its meaning is muḥsib, that is, sufficient. Some of them denied that fi'āl forms come from verbs, and that dirāk comes from darak; so let this be examined.

Shurayḥ ibn Yazīd al-Ḥimṣī and Abu al-Barahsam read it with a kasrah on the ḥā' and a shaddah on the sīn, as a verbal noun like kiddhāb.

Ibn 'Abbās read ﴿ḥusnan﴾ with a nūn, from ḥusn (goodness).

Al-Mahdawī reported ﴿ḥasban﴾ with a fatḥah on the ḥā', a sukūn on the sīn and the letter bā', like your saying: ḥasbuka kadhā, meaning: it suffices you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 37:

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the word ﴿your Lord﴾, and in its being a substitute there is an evident magnification and an allusion to what is said, as opposed to what is related in the books of the Sufis, of the sacred hadith: "Were it not for you, the spheres would not have been created."

And His, exalted is He, saying ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ is an attribute (sifah) of ﴿your Lord﴾ or of ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾, according to the most correct view of the muhaqqiqun (the verifying scholars), regarding the permissibility of describing a noun in genitive construction (mudaf) that is attached to a definite noun by the definite article. It is also permitted that it be an explicative apposition ('atf bayan). Can it be a substitute for the word "your Lord"? Al-Bahr says: "There is consideration in this, because the apparent view is that a substitute is not repeated."

His, exalted is He, saying ﴿They will not possess from Him any address﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf muqarrir) confirming what the general lordship implies of utmost greatness, and the independence of Him, exalted is He, in what has been mentioned of recompense and bestowal, without anyone having any power over it. This reading is narrated from 'Abdullah, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'mash, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim. Al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu 'Amr and the two Haramis (the scholars of Mecca and Medina) read both nouns in the nominative (raf'), and it is said: they are two predicates of an implied subject, i.e., He is the Lord of the heavens, etc. It is said: the first is the predicate and the second is its attribute or explicative apposition. It is said: the first is the subject and the second is its predicate. ﴿They do not possess from Him﴾ is another predicate, or it is the predicate and the second is an attribute of the first or an explicative apposition. It is said: (they do not possess) is a necessary circumstantial clause (hal lazimah). It is said: the first is the first subject, the second is a second subject, and (they do not possess) is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of the first; the connection is achieved by repeating the subject with its meaning, according to the opinion of those who hold this. It is preferred that both be nominative by way of praise (madh), or that the second be an attribute of the first, and (they do not possess) be a resumptive clause as it stands, because of the agreement of the two readings in meaning. Al-Akhawan, al-Hasan, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and Ibn Muhaysin, with a variant from two of them, read the first in the genitive (jarr), as you have heard, and the second in the nominative (raf') as a new subject, with the predicate being what follows it; or as a predicate of an implied subject, with what follows being a resumptive clause; or as a second predicate. The pronoun in (they do not possess) refers to the people of the heavens and the earth, and (from Him) explains ﴿address﴾, placed before it; that is: they do not possess the ability to address Him, exalted and majestic, of their own accord, as the word "possess" indicates, any address whatsoever. The intent is the negation of their ability to address Him, mighty and majestic, with anything concerning the lessening of punishment or the increase of reward, without His permission, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. It is also permitted that "from Him" be connected to (they do not possess), with "min" being the min of origin, and the meaning: they do not possess from God, exalted is He, any address; that is, God, exalted is He, does not grant them ownership of this, so there is not in their hands any address which they could dispose of as owners dispose, so that they might increase the reward or decrease the punishment. This is like saying: "I possess a dirham from him," and it is less forced and more apparent than making (from Him) a circumstantial clause of ﴿address﴾ placed before it, with an implied genitive construction; that is, an address from the address of God, exalted is He, so that the meaning becomes: they do not possess one address from among all that God, exalted is He, is addressed with and commands regarding reward and punishment. The apparent sense of al-Baydawi's words is to take "address" as the address of objection against Him, glorified is He, regarding reward or punishment; and from Him, as we heard from us earlier, they do not possess addressing Him, exalted is He, nor objecting to Him, glorified is He, regarding reward or punishment, because they are owned by Him, exalted and majestic, absolutely, so they have no right whatsoever to object to Him, glorified is He. Whichever is the case, the verse is not suitable as evidence for negating intercession with His permission, exalted and majestic. It is narrated from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, that the pronoun in ﴿they do not possess﴾ refers to the polytheists, and the unsuitability of it as evidence is more apparent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 78, verse 38:

﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾. It is said: "the Spirit" is a creation greater than the angels, more noble than them, and nearer to the Lord of the Worlds. It is also said: it is an angel, and God, Mighty and Majestic, has created nothing greater than it after the Throne. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when the Day of Resurrection comes, it will stand alone in a row, and the angels in a row. It is related from al-Dahhak that if it opened its mouth, it would fill all the angels, peace be upon them.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Spirit is one of the armies of God, the Exalted. They are not angels. They have heads, hands and feet."

In another narration: "They eat food." Then he recited: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾, and said: "These are an army, and those are an army."

This view is also related from Mujahid and Abu Salih. It is said: they are the noblest of the angels. It is said: they are the guardian angels. It is said: they are an angel appointed over the spirits. In al-Ihya' (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din) it is said: "The angel called the Spirit is the one who breathes the spirits into the bodies. He breathes, and with each of his breaths a spirit enters a body. This is a truth that the masters of the hearts witness with their insight." Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Dahhak that it is Gabriel, peace be upon him, and this is also an opinion of Ibn 'Abbas. Indeed, he (Ibn 'Abbas) also related from him that he said: "Gabriel, peace be upon him, will stand on the Day of Resurrection in a row before the Almighty, his limbs trembling with fear of the punishment of God, the Exalted. He will say: 'Glory be to You, there is no god but You. We did not worship You as You deserve to be worshipped.' The distance between his shoulders is as the distance between the East and the West. Have you not heard the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾?"

In al-Bayhaqi's narration in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat from him, the intended meaning is the spirits of people, and their standing with the angels is between the two blasts, before they are returned to the bodies. This is very contrary to the apparent meaning of the verse, and perhaps it is not authentically transmitted from the learned Ibn 'Abbas. It is said: the Qur'an and its standing is a metaphor for the manifestation of its effects, which arise from affirming it or denying it. In this there is a combination of the literal and the figurative, with what is not hidden. In my view, nothing authentic has been established here.

"Day" (yawm) is an adverbial complement of ﴿they will not have power﴾ (78:37), and "in rows" (saffan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: lined up. It is said: they are two rows, the Spirit being one row, whether singular or multiple, and the angels another row. It is also said: they are rows, and this is the most suitable, due to His saying: ﴿and the angel in rows upon rows﴾ (89:22). It is said: all of them, the Spirit and the angels, are one row. It is also permitted that it be an adverbial complement of His saying ﴿they shall not speak﴾ and His saying: ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and who says what is right﴾ (78:38), as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in ﴿they shall not speak﴾, which refers to the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, among whom are the Spirit and the angels. The mention of their standing in rows is to confirm the greatness of His sovereignty, the majesty of His lordship, Mighty and Majestic, and to inspire awe for the Day of Resurrection, around which the discourse revolves from the beginning to the end of this noble surah. The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming the content of His saying: ﴿they will not have power﴾, and emphasizing it, meaning that the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, when on that day they are unable to speak anything of the kind of speech, except one whom God, the Exalted, permits among them to speak in general, and that permitted one says, by a partial permission in speaking generally, something right, that is, true, concerning intercession for whomever He is pleased with. How then could they have power to address the Lord of Might, may His majesty be exalted, when that is more specific than general speech and more precious in its aim?

It is also permitted that the pronoun in ﴿they shall not speak﴾ refers to "the Spirit and the angels", and the sentence confirms the content of His saying: ﴿they will not have power﴾ as well, but with the meaning that the Spirit and the angels, despite being the best of creation and nearest to God, the Exalted, if they cannot speak what is right of intercession for whomever He is pleased with, except with His permission, then how could anyone else have power over it?

Some of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) mentioned this, and it was criticized as being based on the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazila) that the angels, peace be upon them, are more excellent than humans in every respect. You know that among the People of the Sunnah too are those who held this, such as Abu 'Abd Allah al-Halimi, the judge Abu Bakr al-Baqillani, and the Imam al-Razi. It is attributed to the judge al-Baydawi, and his words in the tafsir here are not free from obscurity. Those who undertook to justify it made long efforts, to the effect that the disagreement over their superiority is in the sense of abundance of reward and what results from it, namely that they are more honored by God, the Exalted, and more beloved to Him, glory be to Him, and not in the sense of nearness of station, entering the sacred enclosures, lifting the veil of the kingdom by being informed of what is hidden from us. The relevant considerations are purity, fewness of intermediaries, and the like, for in this respect they are more excellent without any disagreement. The words of that party may be understood as being based on this. This is like what we witness in the condition of the servants of a king, and especially his inner household, for they are nearer to him than his ministers and those who are outside of his relatives, yet they are not of one rank with him, even if they exceed in familiarity and intimacy with him.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the pronoun in ﴿they shall not speak﴾ refers to humankind. It is also permitted that ﴿except one whom He permits﴾ etc. be in the accusative as an exception in its basic sense, and the meaning is: they shall not speak except concerning a person whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and that person says, in the world, what is right, that is, true, which is the Oneness of God and the statement "There is no god but God," as is related from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Accordingly, it has been said:

It is permitted that ﴿and who says what is right﴾ be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) for the one who is, with "qad" implied or not, and not as a conjunction with ﴿permits﴾. Some people permitted the circumstantial reading in the first sense as well, but from the pronoun in ﴿they shall not speak﴾, considering each one individually or considering the whole group. They supposed that the statement of some of them, that the meaning is "they shall not speak what is right except by His permission," would not be complete without that, but in it there is what there is. It has been said: the clause ﴿they shall not speak﴾ is a circumstantial clause for ﴿the Spirit and the angels﴾, or for their pronoun in ﴿in rows﴾. The majority hold to what has preceded.

The explicit mention of "the Most Merciful" in the place where a pronoun would be expected is to indicate that the basis of permission is the all-encompassing mercy, not that anyone deserves it from Him, glory be to Him and exalted. Likewise, His mention before in the allusive form indicates that mercy is the basis of His nurturing, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the day of their rising in the manner described, and it carries the sense of distance together with the nearness of the time of what is referred to, to signal the elevation of its rank and the remoteness of its station in terror and grandeur. Its position is nominative as a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and its predicate is His, the Exalted's, statement: ﴿the Day﴾, described by His, the Glorified's, words: ﴿the Truth﴾. Or it may be that the predicate is "the good". The word "اليوم" is either a substitute (badal) or an explicative apposition (`atf bayan). By "the Truth" is meant what is firmly established and certain; that is, that Day is the established, certainly occurring event. The sentence serves to emphasize what precedes it, which is why it is not joined by a conjunction. The fa' in His, the Mighty and Majestic, statement: ﴿So whoever wills takes a return to his Lord﴾ is elocutionary (fa-sihiyyah, a particle that makes an implied condition explicit), revealing a omitted condition. The object of "wills" is omitted, and it is indicated by the apodosis. ﴿To his Lord﴾ is attached to what precedes it, to give it emphasis and to observe the rhyme (fawasil). It is as if it were said: since the matter is as mentioned, the aforementioned event being certain to occur, whoever wills to take a place of return to the reward of his Lord, whose great station has been mentioned, let him do so through faith and obedience.

Qatada said, as transmitted from him by Abd ibn Humayd, Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir: ﴿ma'ab﴾ means "a way". The preposition is attached to it because it carries the sense of leading to and conveying. The first view is more apparent. The noun that is omitted, namely "the reward", is supposed to be understood because a return to the Essence of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, is impossible. It has also been said that the return of every person to his Lord, the Glorified, is not by his own will, since it is necessary whether he wills it or not. What is conditional on the will is the return to His reward, the Exalted, for the servant is free to choose faith and obedience, and there is no reward without them. It has also been said that the omission is due to the preceding statement of the Exalted: ﴿For the transgressors there is an evil place of return﴾, for they too have a return to Allah, the Exalted, but it is for punishment and not for reward. Each view has its own perspective.

﴿Indeed, We have warned you﴾, i.e., by what has been mentioned in the surah of the verses that speak of resurrection, with what is in it and what follows it of calamities, or by them and by all the catastrophes (al-qawari'ah) that occur in the Mighty Qur'an.

﴿a near punishment﴾: It is the punishment of the Hereafter, and its nearness is due to the certainty of its coming. It has been said: "How far is what has passed, and how near is what is coming." Or it is near in relation to Him, Mighty and Majestic. Or it may be said: the barzakh (the intermediate state) is included in the Hereafter, and its beginning is death, and it is truly near, as is not hidden from one who understands nearness and distance. From Qatadah: it is the punishment for sin, because it is the nearer of the two punishments. From Muqatil: it is the killing of the Quraysh on the day of Badr. This has been objected to on the grounds that the saying of Him, Exalted, ﴿the day when a person sees what his hands have sent forward﴾ rejects it, for the apparent reading is that it is an adverbial complement (zarf) of an implied element that is an attribute of "punishment"; i.e., a punishment existing on the day of... etc. That day is none other than the Day of Resurrection. The same applies to what has been said, that it is a substitute for "punishment," or an adverbial complement of "near."

On this last view it has been said: there is no need to justify the nearness, because the punishment on that day is near, with no barrier between it and the person. This was examined by saying that the apparent reading is to make the thing warned of near at the time of warning, because that suits intimidation and threat; for there is no benefit in mentioning its nearness to them on the Day of Resurrection. When it is connected to that day, the purpose is to explain the nearness of the day itself. So reflect.

It is apparent that ﴿the person (al-mar')﴾ is general, covering both the believer and the disbeliever. "Ma" is a relative pronoun in the accusative governed by ﴿sees (yanzuru)﴾, and the returning pronoun is omitted; the meaning is: on the day when the responsible person, believer and disbeliever alike, witnesses what he has sent forward of good or evil. It has also been permitted that "ma" be an interrogative in the accusative governed by ﴿sent forward (qaddamat)﴾, i.e., he sees what his hands have sent forward, and the clause is suspended (mu'allaq), since seeing is a way of knowing; the verb ﴿sees﴾ in the saying is the response to "what his hands have sent forward." In the discourse, according to what the Allamah al-Taftazani mentioned, there is a figure of speech (taghlib) in which what occurred in a particular manner is given precedence over what occurred in other than that manner, in that the two hands are mentioned, because most deeds are performed with them; so all of them are treated as if done with them, by way of taghlib.

Ibn Abi Ishaq read "al-mur'" with a damma on the mim. Abu Hatim considered it weak, but it should not be deemed weak, for it is the dialect of some Arabs who make the vowel of the hamza follow the vowel of the case-ending, so they say: mar'un, mar'an, and mar'in, according to the i'rab (grammatical inflection).

﴿And the disbeliever will say: "Oh, would that I had been dust!"﴾ This singles out one of the two groups that the word "the person" previously encompassed, by mentioning it specifically. The saying of the disbeliever is singled out rather than that of the believer, because his saying indicates the utmost disappointment and the extreme of regret, and the omission of the saying of the believers indicates the utmost exultation and the extreme of joy and delight. Ata' said: "the person" here means the disbeliever, because of the saying of Him, Exalted: ﴿Indeed We have warned you﴾; and the apparent reading would be the pronoun in what follows, but he placed the explicit noun in its place to increase the reproach. In this is the point that the inclusion of both groups is the one that corresponds to what preceded of the description of a day that distinguishes, comprising the condition of both; and this is the meaning of the saying of Him, Exalted: ﴿So whoever wills may take to his Lord a return﴾, and ﴿Indeed We have warned you﴾.

It does not restrict it to the disbeliever, because the warning is general to both groups as well, so there is no indication of restriction. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Hasan said: what is meant by it is the believer. The Imam said: what indicates this is the saying of the disbeliever, for since that was an explanation of the condition of the disbeliever, the first must be an explanation of the condition of the believer. The weakness of this is not hidden, like the argument of al-Riyashi using the verse to show that "al-mar'" is applied only to the believer.

By his saying "Oh, would that I had been dust!" the disbeliever meant either: in the world, so that I had not been created and had not been made responsible; or: would that I had been dust on this day, so that I had not been resurrected. From Ibn Umar, Abu Hurayrah and Mujahid: Allah, Exalted, brings the animals together, and He exacts retribution for some of them from others; then He, Glorified, says to them: "Be dust," and all of them become dust. When the disbeliever sees that, he wishes for the like of it. The majority went to the gathering of animals and the exacting of retribution for some from others, and the discussion of that will come in the surah of al-Takwir, if Allah, Exalted, wills. It has been said: the disbeliever in the verse is Iblis, may the curse be upon him; when he witnessed Adam, peace be upon him, and his believing offspring, and the reward they had, he wished to be dust, because he had despised Adam when he said: ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾. This is far from the context, though it is good. Dust, in all that has been mentioned, bears its well-known meaning, and the statement is to be taken in its apparent and literal sense. It has also been permitted, especially on the last view, that what is meant by the saying "would that I had been in the world" is being humble in obedience to Allah, Exalted, not tyrannical or arrogant. What is relied upon is what has preceded, as is not hidden.
